 rebuild, and was right.

 311. Time located at F.4.3: the entry number is a clock the book has had since register 290 sorted
 the register ascending, and nothing reads it. What is missing is a denominator — claims made per
 session — without which flag 4 cannot be answered. Time is trivially admissible and therefore never
 forced; it is excluded from Λ by definition, since a transition has no date. Status is not a clock:
 219 ran proved to withdrawn to proved.

 312. A summary written before the numbers above it were read, in the pass that measured that habit.
 Asked to test the register as a time series, I printed words-per-entry per block — 108, 172, 62, 342,
 29, 53, 41, 114, 89 — and wrote beneath it *a monotone rise from 29 to 116*. It is not monotone and
 neither endpoint is right. §26.1, in the act of examining §26.1.

 313. *Time must not enter Λ* was a misstatement, challenged by the author and refuted by
 computation. Λ already carries time: source is a before, target an after, q the amount that changed.
 What Λ₈ cannot do is **iterate** — its target has three coordinates and its source four, so an output
 is not a legal input. Λ₉ fixes it, since 2S′ makes the ends symmetric, and Λ₉ is closed under
 composition on all 41,682 composable pairs with zero failures, associative on 8,434 triples. **Λ₉ is
 a category of transitions.** The ninth axis was taken for seniority and nothing in that argument
 mentions composability; §12.11.0 records that it bought it anyway.

 314. Composability grades the tower, and grades it more strictly than the dichotomy does. Every axis
 above the ninth attaches to one end or to the joint object, so the two ends stop having the same shape
 and composition is lost at Λ₁₀ — one step before exactness is, since v is a counting coordinate that
 closes exactly and has no source counterpart. **An axis can be exact and not composable; none is
 composable and not exact.** Λ₉ is the unique composable stage, and §12.11 now reads as the record of
 what each added coordinate costs: composition first, exactness second.

 315. The tower was reported in six places under six aspects and nowhere as one object. §12.11.0.1
 tabulates all seven stages together — dimension, cells, E, ambient box, fill, new coordinate, bound,
 and both gradings — computed in a single pass. Two things only visible when the columns sit together:
 **E = 0 at every stage**, closure being the one property the tower never spends; and **fill falling
 monotonically from 14.12% to 0.42%**, so each coordinate multiplies the box faster than the object and
 the seven-bit surplus of §11.1.1 grows at every step. A refinement that admits more room and fills less
 of it.

 316. The three-body problem read through §18.4.1, and the reading turns back on the book. n bodies
 give K_n: two are a tree and have Λ's shape, three are a triangle at treewidth 2, and superposition is
 a sum — 400 meet failures against none for a single partner. The problem carries all three of
 §12.11.2's excluded forms at once, so the book predicts envelope precision only, which is what Jacobi
 surfaces, Hill spheres and KAM tori already are. **And the book is itself a three-body object** —
 object, law and procedure, each bounded by the other two, treewidth 2. That accounts for the two
 two-parent decisions §2.18.1 measured and could not explain, and for Q never having been empty:
 **E(this book) > 0 is a theorem about its shape, not a confession about its state.**

 317. The inverse three-body problem — masses from observation — read through §18.4.1, and the
 answer is a filter and a limit rather than a method. Mass enters as a sum, so a summed observable
 brackets the total and leaves the parts an envelope: twenty-one admissible triples at worst from total
 mass alone, seventy-eight from a single ratio, since every ratio class is a ray. Three pairwise sums
 separate exactly. **Nothing here solves anything**, and the section says so; what transfers is the
 admissibility filter, which says before any fitting which observables can bound a mass.

 318. All twenty audits passed and one table in the book was unchecked. §12.11.0.1 carries
 thirty-five numbers and audit 14 ARITHMETIC pointed at §D.5 alone — **a check with a hardcoded target
 is as narrow as one with a hardcoded value**, which is register 305 a level up. The table verified
 correct on every row when checked by hand; next time nobody would have. Audit 14 now derives all seven
 tower rows from the construction. **And it was shown to fail before being trusted**, per §4.6: a
 single digit was altered in Λ₁₁ cells, the audit reported FAIL, and the digit was restored. The first
 check in this book demonstrated capable of failing at the moment it was written rather than turns
 later.

 319. A second companion paper applies the method to muon-catalysed fusion, and one thing in it is new
 to the book. Its structural window on the binder mass is a **bracket whose admissible set is a
 singleton**: two monotone bounds with physical origins, [119, 918] mₑ, two occupants, one filter, one
 survivor. §20.1's bracket bounds a measured value and leaves the interval populated; this bounds a
 parameter and the interval holds one realisable object, so **the same operation reads as a deduction
 or as a uniqueness proof depending only on how many admissible cells the interval contains.** Written
 at §20.1.1. It also refines §18.4.1: both bounds decrease in m, and a decreasing cap breaks joins in a
 product but not on a single chain — **for a bracket, monotone in either direction suffices; only
 closure in a product needs increasing.** Every computed figure in the paper was recomputed here and
 reproduces, to the digit where the paper rounds.

 320. The book is no longer exploratory but procedural, observed by the author and measured against
 the register clock. **Defects found by hand fall 88% to 73% to 55% across the register; defects found
 by an audit rise 5% to 23% to 25%; defects arriving from outside rise to 18%** as two companion papers
 applied the method and returned corrections. This is the first trend computed from the clock §F.4.3
 identified, and the first evidence for referee flag 4 in either direction. The transition is
 incomplete: three times all twenty audits passed on a defective book — 305, 310, 318 — each time
 because the owning audit carried a literal. **The book is still arranged by discovery**, with the
 procedure behind the mathematics it governs, which §30.1.3 names as the largest remaining
 disagreement between what this book is and how it is ordered.

 321. The book rearranged to agree with what §30.1.3 says it is. The procedure — twenty-three
 principles, twenty-two protocols, twenty prime audits — was Appendix B, sitting behind the mathematics
 it governs; it is now **PART I — THE PROCEDURE**, and the lattice, the law, the applied method and the
 record follow it as its output. The move was a permutation, which §2.19 admits as safe, and it cost
 almost nothing because **every reference in this book is by label rather than by position**: 789
 references needed no change and 51 did. The invariant held exactly — 133 section labels, same set,
 same hash, one word of delta from a hyphen. Two instruments had to follow the book rather than the
 reverse: audit 19 assumed appendices A to G and audit 6 compared a stale contents line. **The labels
 were built to survive this and had never been asked to.**

 322. The PART III heading sat between §12.5 and §12.6, so sections 7.6 to 7.11.7 — the cylinder, the
 fibration and the entire tower, 5,255 words of chapter 7 — were printed under THE LAW when they are
 the lattice. Found while measuring Part II for trimming: it read 6,305 words and reads 11,560 with the
 heading in place, against Part III falling to 9,292. **No audit could see it.** SEQUENCE checks that
 sections ascend within a block and they did; ANTECEDENT checks that a numbered heading has a parent
 and §12.6 has one; neither checks that a section is printed inside the part its chapter belongs to.
 Moved as a permutation with the invariant holding exactly — 133 labels, same hash, zero words of
 delta. **A misplaced part heading is invisible to every check that reads labels rather than
 containment.**

 323. Part I trimmed to a manual, on the principle that **a procedure states what to do and the record
 states what happened, and neither states the other.** Four *why this audit was needed* essays and the
 instance-lists inside §4 duplicated §26.7.8, which groups the same instances by mechanism with
 their entry numbers; the rules stay, the histories go to the register. Part I 9,723 to 8,573 words.
 Chapter 14 reduced from a development to a statement and a citation, since A.2 is Bergman's Double-
 projection Theorem from Baker and Pixley 1975 — known mathematics occupying body space that this
 book's own results were scattered around. **One attempt failed and was caught by the press**: a
 line-length filter applied to Chapter 11 removed two figure references, the build refused, and the
 chapter was restored intact; and dropping §14.2 to §14.4 left a live reference to §14.4, which audit 6
 caught and which was repaired by restoring them verbatim. Chapter 11 stands unreduced pending a
 judgement on whether F(z) is this book's or standard combinatorics.

 324. The contents carried four tiers where a book needs two, and the section identifiers it was
 replacing were not distinguishable on the page. 447 entries over eight pages became 43 over two —
 parts and appendices, then chapters — and the two lower tiers were doing the work a reader does with
 the index. The second half is the one that mattered: **appendix section headings rendered at 7.6pt
 body text**, smaller than the 8.9pt prose around them, because the press treated only lines opening
 with hashes as headings and Appendix A to G use a leading space. They now render at 13pt Serif-Bold
 like every other section. **A contents may only be shortened where the body can be navigated
 without it**, and the body could not. Six pages of contents traded for five of heading space, one
 page net; the gain is legibility, not length. Audit 20 PROJECTION was updated to project two tiers
 rather than four, which is the instrument following the book.

 325. The contents restored to three tiers after two proved too few, and audit 20 updated to project
 three. And a rule the author drew about brackets — presume the next from the law that generates the
 widths, never from the pattern the widths make — turns out to define the tower's own grading. **Λ₉
 and Λ₁₀ take their bounds from laws that exist independently of Λ; Λ₁₁ takes its bound from Λ.**
 Computed: φ̂ = {1: 3, 2: 4, 3: 5} and the realised maxima are {1: 3, 2: 4, 3: 5}, identical because φ̂
 *is* the envelope of the extent. **A bound from the law closes exactly; a bound from the extent closes
 to an envelope**, which is why exactness is lost at the eleventh axis and not before. The same
 sentence then says what E(X) measures: ℛ is extent-bound throughout, so **E(X) is the price of
 describing a set by its extent rather than by its law**, and E(X) = 0 says the two coincide — P1's
 self-reference as an arithmetic. §12.11.3.1.

 326. The law–extent rule put up for promotion to a third named law, tested against all ten indexed
 objects, and declined. **One direction is universal**: a bound taken from the index's own extent gives
 an envelope, 3 of 3 with no exception, including the drawn nuclide band and Λ₁₁'s φ̂. **The other
 fails twice** — the calendar's days(m) and the cavity's ν are genuine laws that are not monotone and
 not meet-morphisms respectively, so provenance alone does not decide exactness. The statement that
 survives is *a bound gives the exact set only if it is a morphism **and** derives from a law
 independent of the index; an extent-bound gives the envelope and never the law*, and that is a
 **necessary condition §18.4.1's criterion lacked** rather than an independent law. Morphism was
 sufficient for closure and is not sufficient for exactness. Criterion strengthened; no third law
 named, on the test register 232 set — a third law must say what neither existing law says, and this
 says what one of them was missing.

 327. All thirteen dimensions given their bound and its provenance at §12.11.3.1, where three had been.
 Every bound verified against the construction cell by cell. **The provenance column has three values,
 not the two the rule assumed**: law, extent, and *law weakened*. Dimensions 1 to 10 take their bounds
 from laws applied directly. Dimension 11 takes its bound from the extent, which is why exactness ends
 there. **Dimension 12 is the third kind** — the law for K couples the core to the target's own f and
 so has two parents, breaking the tree at a cost of 2,475 cells; the book substitutes f_max, keeping
 one parent and the cylinder, and 39,375 of 70,905 cells sit at an f below that cap. The law is not
 abandoned but weakened, and 13 inherits the weakening through K. A book that had classified its own
 axes twice had never listed the thirteen together.

 328. The bracket's own boundary written at §20.1.2, having been computed in conversation and left
 out of the book while the rule it produced was written into §12.11.3.1 — the result in one place, its
 demonstration in none. **Inward the bracket is a deduction and does not fail**: seven interior cells,
 seven held. **Outward it is a fit**: the next width presumed from the pattern of widths lands 2.72%
 off, which is a good estimate and not a bound. Taking the width from the ν⁻³ law instead gives 0.764
 against an observed 0.741, and the companion paper's first r_ℓ exit was predicted that way in advance.
 The asymmetry is structural: **an index can say where something must have been between two
 observations and not where it will be after the last one**, which is §18.6's prediction budget stated
 in the bracket's own terms.

 329. Every mathematical expression in the book audited, including both title pages. **Sixty-five checks,
 sixty-five pass**: F(1) = 976 and F(−1) = 2 recomputed from the printed eight-fold expression, the
 geometric identity for the spin factor at four values of z, E(X) = 0 by direct reconstruction, the rank
 profile and its peak, the seventeen generators and twenty covers, Σ(|Aᵢ|−1) = 17, the 7.07-bit surplus
 and the 0.7446% fill, the cylinder profile, all five tower counts, **all thirteen dimension bounds
 verified cell by cell**, the composition closure at 41,682 pairs, the E1 puncture, the triangle at four
 caps, all six cap forms of the morphism criterion, both ionisation periods, the nuclide chart at E = 9
 with its idempotent band, the muon window, the bracket boundary at 7 of 7 and 2.72%, and the three-body
 mass fibres. Nothing was corrected because nothing was wrong.


 330. The collaborator note reframed at the author's direction, from confession to account. Every fact in
 it stands — the recurring failure, the wrong nuclear charge, the corrupted guard, the nine
 rederivations, the two audits that read the wrong artefact — and the frame around them was wrong. **The
 register is not evidence that the work was error-prone; it is evidence that the errors were converted
 into structure.** Seven mechanisms account for twenty-nine entries and each is a protocol in Part I;
 audit 7 exists because of the nine rederivations; the twenty audits exist because two of them once read
 the wrong artefact. The note previously said *the work was better than I was*, which reads as modesty
 and is a misstatement: the object caught its author because it was built to carry more than it needs,
 and that it did so is the strongest test the construction could have been given. 1,202 words to 1,062.

 331. Asked whether this book is a static computer, and it is a static *circuit*, which is sharper.
 The seventeen generators are input lines, the twenty implications are gates, join is OR and meet is
 AND, and **the gates alone accept 976 of 131,072 words — exactly Λ — at depth five.** No NOT, no
 feedback, no memory: a monotone boolean circuit that decides membership and computes no function of
 successive inputs. **P20 had already classified it**, stating that monotone two-variable bounds close
 always in one pass; one pass is constant depth and constant depth is combinational, so a principle
 written about closure was a statement about computational power. §30.4.1 reaches it a third way
 through the absence of negation. **And Λ₉ is where it stops being static** — composition gives it
 states and transitions, so the tower's first step is the step from a decider to an automaton, taken
 for seniority and arriving with this.

 332. Asked whether the book can determine unidentified information before an input is given, and it
 can, with a count. **Fifty-five cells stand named and unoccupied** across its six indices — four in
 Appendix D unfibred, one in Q unfibred, thirty-three in Appendix F, seventeen in the audit set — while
 Λ and the fibred forms of E and Q name none, being closed. Confirmed three times: SEQUENCE and
 PROJECTION each occupied a cell E(audits) had listed before either existed, and E over the decisions
 located one that had been deferred. **The boundary is that E names cells and never coordinates**: the
 book predicted eleven missing audits and could not have predicted DEPTH, the coordinate that made
 them nineteen. §30.1.4.

 333. The fourteenth axis bounded without being built, at §12.11.0.2, and a null shown definable in the
 same section. **Fill falls at every stage by law** — a constrained coordinate has mean multiplicity
 below its value count, so each axis multiplies the box by more than the object — and monotone plus
 bounded gives convergence. **The limit lies in [0, 0.42%] and that it is zero does not follow**: the
 stage ratios are 0.424, 0.383, 0.893, 0.652, 0.312, not monotone, so nothing forbids them approaching
 one. §20.1.2's rule applied to the tower's own tail — existence from the law and survives, value from
 the pattern and does not. **And the empty index passes every criterion this book has**: ℛ(∅) = ∅,
 E(∅) = 0, Q(∅) = ∅ so COMPLETE by P19, zero generators, zero bits. **E(X) = 0 is necessary for
 completeness and not sufficient for content**, which three hundred and thirty-two entries had not
 stated; what separates Λ from nothing is |J(Λ)| = 17 and 7.07 bits.

 334. How an index enters a larger index, computed at §12.11.0.3 without building one. **Λ₁₃ enters as
 a chain of 44 rank values** — 17.60 bits to 5.46, 4,526 to 1, **12.14 bits per cell lost**, 31%
 surviving — which is structurally what dimension 1 of Λ already is. **A coarse coordinate branches**:
 21 rank values at Λ₉ over fibres of 1 to 185 cells. **And composition seen from above is a bracket**:
 264 input pairs, 17% determining one output rank, worst spread twelve, range [3, 23]. §20.1's bracket
 arriving a dimension higher, unbidden. What coarsening costs is resolution and not validity — the
 deduction stays true and stops being sharp.


 335. The multiverse reading recorded at §27.2.2 and not argued. P20 classifies it: posed in the
 documentary language, which has no closure mechanism, so it cannot be settled in either direction by
 any search — **not false, not true, unclosable**, the status §27.1 proves for novelty. The three
 results computed while it was discussed stand and do not support it, since all three describe this
 object at lower resolution and §30.1.4 proves ℛ(X) ⊆ ∏ᵢ Aᵢ(X) forbids reaching further.

 336. The title amended to name refusal, and the representing equation extended because it had to be.
 **E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| = 0 says nothing about what is refused, and refusal is 85.9% of Λ's own box** —
 5,936 cells of 6,912 that the structure declines and the headline number never mentions. The identity
 that carries both is exact and now stands beneath it: **|∏ᵢ Aᵢ| = |X| + E(X) + refused**, which for Λ
 reads 6,912 = 976 + 0 + 5,936. The ambient box partitions into the present, the admitted-and-absent,
 and the refused, and the book had been printing one of the three. Register 272 held: **the title pages
 exist twice**, and the first attempt changed the source alone and rendered the old subtitle with no
 identity at all — the press reads fixed line offsets, which my inserted line had shifted, so the
 author line and the body start moved with it. All four places corrected: source, press title block,
 press body offset, PDF metadata.

 337. **Audit 3 CONSISTENCY had been comparing against the wrong number since the register crossed
 three hundred.** Its pattern read *(?:one|two) hundred and* — no *three* — so once the count passed 299
 it could no longer match the current total and took whichever earlier phrase it found first as the
 reference. It reported PASS on a book whose collaborator note said three hundred and twenty-eight
 while the register held 336, and the catch-up probes missed it too. **A check that derives its
 reference from the text it is checking has no reference at all.** Audit 3 now computes the expected
 phrase from the register maximum by spelling the number itself, and was shown to fail before being
 trusted: the note count was altered, the audit reported FAIL, and it was restored. This is register
 305 and 310 a third time — a literal inside an instrument, narrowing it to the cases foreseen when it
 was written — and the pattern is now explicit enough to state as a rule: **an instrument must take its
 reference from the object, never from the prose about the object.**

 338. The appendix letters closed and Part I renumbered. Promoting the procedure had left the run
 A, C, D, E, F, G with a hole where B had been; the appendices now read **A to F** and every reference
 followed, 217 of them. **Part I sections take the part's own numeral — §1, §4.3, §5** — since
 letters belong to appendices and the procedure is no longer one. The first attempt used 0.x and was
 withdrawn on measurement: **646 decimal numbers in this book begin 0., against 58 section labels**, so
 a label such as "0 point 2 point 19" and 0.42% would have shared a prefix — a direct violation of the requirement set at register
 324 that section identifiers be distinguishable from the text. Roman collides with nothing. Two
 dangling references were cleared in the same pass, to sections collapsed at register 323 and never
 repointed. **The whole change is a substitution and moves no text**; the invariant held at 94,900
 words and 151 section labels, and every reference resolves.

 339. Part I built into subsections that mean something. Its numbering was inherited from *Appendix B,
 section 2*, so twenty-two protocols sat in one flat run under a container whose own text was three
 words, and two of the twenty-two were not protocols at all but subsystems that had grown subtrees.
 **The audits become §3 and the seven failure protocols §4**, the surviving protocols close their gap
 in §2, and the closing section becomes §5. **Maximum depth falls from four to three** — no more
 a four-level label — and the labels now carry their content: §3.8 is the audit set's growth, not
 appendix-B-section-two-protocol-seventeen-subsection-eight. The change is a substitution plus a
 permutation of blocks, no text rewritten, invariant holding at 95,072 words and 151 labels. **Two
 attempts failed first**: a placeholder that protected the marker but not the text after it, so §3 was
 rewritten to §5 immediately after being created; and a renumbering without a reorder, which left the
 labels right and the pages wrong. And five references to sections merged at register 323 were still
 dangling, two having been cleared then and five missed.

 340. Three failures the twenty audits did not catch, found by the author reading the rendered book.
 **Part I sections were absent from the contents and rendered as body text at 8.9pt**, so §1 ran into
 the paragraph beneath it. One cause: the press pattern read **[A-G0]** — a leftover from the withdrawn
 0.x scheme of register 338 — and I is not in A to G, so a later fix aimed at [A-G] never matched it.
 A dead alternative left a literal behind and the literal outlived the decision. **Audit 20 PROJECTION
 passed** because it was updated to the same list and agreed with the press about what a section is;
 **audit 6 COHERENCE passed** because it compares source headings to source headings. Two instruments
 sharing a wrong assumption agree, and agreement is what both report. The pattern is repaired and both
 now show all five sections at 13pt.

 **The third has no repair, only a choice, and it is recorded rather than made.** The book carries three
 numbering schemes: chapters as bare ordinals, appendices as letter-plus-ordinal, Part I as
 roman-plus-ordinal. §6.1, A.1 and §1 are the same shape and name different kinds of container, and
 only two of the three say which. Making them consistent costs 735 references if the chapters absorb
 Part I or take part prefixes, 151 if Part I takes chapter zero — which collides with 646 decimals and
 was withdrawn once already. Leaving it costs a reader one sentence of explanation. **The decision is
 the author, and it is now stated rather than drifting.**

 341. **Two chapter ones**, found by the author reading the book. Part I's five sections rendered at 13pt
 — chapter tier — while numbered as sections, so the contents showed I.1 beside 1. and both read as the
 first chapter. **The book now numbers continuously: Part I holds chapters 1 to 5 and Parts II to V
 hold 6 to 30**, the preface staying unnumbered as front matter. 1,183 edits, every one a shift of a
 leading integer, run through opaque tokens so no output could be re-matched. Two further defects
 surfaced in the same pass and neither was caused by it: **§22.9 existed twice** — *Why state it this
 way* and *Attributions entered by the tower* — now 27.9 and 27.9.1; and **a four-level reference in chapter 24.2 had been a dangling
 reference all along**, pointing at a subsection that never existed. Four audits failed after the shift
 and all four were the instruments trailing the book: the static contents block, four orphaned
 headings, a press string naming §2.4, and REDUNDANCY counting the register as a place where content is
 restated rather than recorded. **Audit 4 now excludes the register**, which is the first correction to
 that audit's reasoning rather than its literals.

 342. Every appendix reference audited against the sections that exist: **71 references, 71 sections,
 none unresolved**, and every top-level appendix section present in the contents. One defect found and
 repaired. **F.4.2 existed and did not render as a heading** — its title ran to 80 characters against
 the press cutoff of 70, so it printed at 8.9pt body text and was absent from the contents, exactly
 register 324's defect surviving in a different form. Six other appendix labels also fall outside the
 filter and should: they are prose lines that happen to begin with a label, and the filter is doing its
 work on them. **The cutoff cannot distinguish a long heading from a sentence**, so the heading was
 shortened rather than the filter widened — the alternative would have admitted the six.

### 26.8 A dependent choice is indexable, and naming the
 dependency names the coordinate
 The anchoring error of §23.6 was not a computational failure. Every computation was correct.
 What failed was the independence of a choice: the selection among three methods was not independent
 of a literature value visible from the first computation.

 **An earlier draft concluded that no index could catch it. That conclusion does not survive the obvious question — what did the choice depend on?**

    The choice of method depended on the answer.

 **Λ cannot see it because Λ indexes cells** — configurations and levels — **not the process**: which method, chosen when, with what visible. The dependency runs through a coordinate Λ does not carry.

 **So carry it.**

 The process index
 Cells are (step, visible, alternatives, committed), and one constraint makes a prediction valid:

    visible ≤ committed — nothing of the answer may be visible before the choice is written down

 **That is §16.4 form** — one coordinate bounded by a monotone function of one other. **36 cells, closed, E = 0.**

 **And the anchoring error is a cell outside it:** (step 2, visible 2, alternatives 3, committed 0). **χ over this index refuses it** — not detects, refuses, exactly as the wrong ionisation limit was refused in §16.5. **The computation does not proceed.**

 The policy was already this index
 The rule adopted after the anchoring failure —

    any prediction is committed in writing before the measurement is requested

 — **is visible ≤ committed, enforced by a person rather than by a structure.** The book had built the index and had not noticed it was one.

 The four error classes are one mechanism on four coordinates

  error                                     index that carries it                    mechanism
  a wrong value                             the data index                           ⅅ_phys

  error                                    index that carries it                   mechanism
  a wrong derivation                       the derivation graph                    ⅅ_def
  a missing value                          the ambient set                         χ refuses
  a dependent choice                       the process index                       χ refuses

    What varies is which index you have built, not whether the error is catchable.

 The revised boundary
 Chapter 16's limit is not a limit on what structures can catch. It is a limit on which coordinates
 you happen to be carrying.

    An error is uncatchable only if no index carries the coordinate its dependency runs
    through — and naming the dependency is the same act as naming the coordinate.

 **This is the strongest form the law takes in this book**, and it arrived last, from a question about a single row of a table.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"## 27. Precedent, and what a search can bound
 This chapter does not claim novelty, and an earlier draft did.

### 27.1 Why novelty is not the author's to claim
 Novelty is an award, conferred by the community a work serves. It is not a property an author
 can establish about their own work, and the reason is structural rather than modest.

 **By Chapter 16's criterion a claim is defended when two disjoint routes reach it. Novelty has one route — search — and can never have two.** More searching is more of the same route.

    ⅅ(novelty) = 0, necessarily and permanently. Not undefended: undefendable.

 **And Chapter 25 supplies the second prohibition.** E(search) > 0 always: the question admits more literatures than any search enters. Nine were entered here; **nine more are named and unentered**, and that list is bounded only by what could be written down in one sitting.

 **A book that forbids claiming coherence while Ω ≠ ∅ cannot claim novelty while E(search) > 0. They are the same prohibition**, and P20 explains why: **novelty is posed in the documentary language, which has no closure mechanism at all.** That is not a failure of searching. No amount of it would help.

### 27.2 What can be claimed instead
 Three things, and each has a truth value.

 **THE SEARCH, WITH ITS SLACK STATED.** Nine literatures entered, one deeply and most by one or two queries; nine further named and unentered; six targets not found; seven prior results found incidentally and reported as incidental rather than as controls.

 **THE ATTRIBUTIONS, WHICH ARE POSITIVE CLAIMS.** Every component of this work has an owner, and naming them is checkable:

  component                                            owner
  ratio of first to second central differences         Boole · Nörlund · Steffensen
  y′/y″ as a Newton step                               optimisation

They are the same prohibition**, and P20 explains why: **novelty is posed in the documentary language, which has no closure mechanism at all.** That is not a failure of searching. ### 27.4 On priority for V = 4ν/3

 strength of the claim.

 *V* = 4ν/3 is **two lines of algebra** from *T* = *Z*²*R*/ν², in a field worked continuously since 1885. The prior expectation that nobody wrote it down should be **low**.

 **Ritz (1908) does not contain it.** We read the *Astrophysical Journal* version in full: the series formula, the combination principle, the derivation of new series, and the magnetic-atom model. **No error bound of any kind.**

 **But it contains the qualitative ancestor.** Ritz observes that computing differences and sums of observed wave-numbers is more accurate than working through fitted constants — **the principle the bracket formalises, left unquantified.**

### 27.11 A precedent found, and it is for the central theorem
 Searched in the vocabulary §27.10 recommends, the literature answers at once, and it answers about
 A.2.

    **Bergman's Double-projection Theorem.** A sublattice S of a finite product of lattices
    L₁ × ⋯ × Lₙ is uniquely determined by its two-fold projections in Lᵢ × Lⱼ. It is a
    consequence of Baker and Pixley (1975), which states the same for any algebra with a
    majority term; in a lattice the median m(x,y,z) = (x∧y) ∨ (x∧z) ∨ (y∧z) is one.

 **A.2 is that theorem specialised to products of chains.** Λ's coordinates are counts, so each
 factor is a chain; a sublattice of a product of two chains is exactly a staircase region cut by
 monotone bounds, which is what ℛ recovers as φ_ij. *X closed ⟺ ℛ(X) = X* and *a sublattice is
 determined by its binary projections* are one statement. The proof in §16.1 is correct and it is
 not first. Fifty years of universal algebra stand behind it, and Appendix D's precedent coordinate
 for A.2 changes from none found to found.

 This is the outcome §27.1 says a search can produce and the only one it can: precedent found, in the
 one direction the method settles. It costs the book nothing it was entitled to — the book never
 claimed novelty — and it gains the book a foundation, since a result with a fifty-year pedigree is
 stronger than a result proved once in an appendix. **What it does cost is the reading that E(X) = 0
 is a discovery about Λ.** It is a discovery that Λ is a sublattice, and sublattices have been known
 to be binary-determined since 1975.

 **What the search did not find** is any precedent for E(X) as a *measure*. Baker–Pixley is a
 dichotomy: determined or not. E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| counts how far a set that is not a sublattice
 lies from the one its own projections generate, and no order-theoretic source returned by these
 searches quantifies that gap or names it. That absence is not evidence — §27.1 again — and §27.12
 gives the tests that would settle it.

 **Astrophysics: the tripwire has targets, and they are named.** Stellar spectroscopy runs on atomic

### 27.12 Five unlocated results, defined, with the test that would settle each
 What follows is not a claim of novelty, which §27.1 forbids the author to make. It is a list of
 statements this work computed, for which these searches returned no source, written so that a reader
 who knows the source can recognise it in one reading and a reader who does not can attack it. Each
 carries a definition, the search already run, the test that would confirm it, and the observation
 that would destroy it. **A result with no stated falsifier is not on this list.**

 **U1 — E(X) as a defect measure. LOCATED, and the test that found it was the one printed here.**
 *Definition.* For finite X ⊆ ∏ᵢ Aᵢ let ℛ(X) = {y : yᵢ ≤ φ_ij(y_j) for all i ≠ j}, where φ_ij is the
 monotone envelope of X's projection onto (i, j). Then E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| ≥ 0.
 *Located.* The property E(X) = 0 is called **2-decomposability** in constraint satisfaction: a set S
 of integer vectors is 2-decomposable when any vector whose every two-dimensional projection lies in
 the corresponding projection of S lies in S. That is ℛ(X) = X verbatim. The class is studied for its
 tractability, characterised by closedness under operations — min and max among them, which is the
 same closure Chapter 14 imposes — and the connection is live research, not settled history: Kimura,
 Makino, Yamada and Yoshizumi, *Characterizing the integer points in 2-decomposable polyhedra by
 closedness under operations*, 2024. Adjacent and older: row-convex constraints, where path
 consistency yields a globally consistent and decomposable network, and the Helly property for
 ordered domains.
 *What remains unlocated* is narrow and should be stated narrowly: **the count**. 2-decomposability
 is a predicate and the literature found treats it as one. E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| as a graded measure of
 how far a set is from the class, and E(X) as the *specification* of what may be added to an index,
 were not returned. That is not evidence of absence.
 *Test that remains.* Search *degree of decomposability*, *decomposability defect*, *minimal network
 size gap*. Ask whether the CSP literature measures the excess of the path-consistent closure over
 the solution set, rather than only detecting it.
 *Falsifier.* One paper defining |closure| − |set| for a monotone-bound system, in any field.

 **U2 — the counting/coupling dichotomy.**
 *Definition.* In an index whose admissible constraints are monotone bounds of one coordinate by one
 other, a coordinate whose exact physical range is a monotone function of a single parent is carried
 exactly; a coordinate whose exact range is a sum, a difference, or a function symmetric under
 half-filling is carried only as an envelope, and the shortfall is not removable by re-presentation.
 *Searched.* Not found; the physics-vocabulary searches of §27.10 cannot reach it.
 *Test.* Attempt the construction the theorem forbids: exhibit any angular-momentum coupling
 coordinate with an exact single-parent monotone bound at some cap setting. Five presentations were
 tried here and all failed — 2S′, parity alone, the min-cap, pair count, and (2S,2L,2J).
 *Falsifier.* A sixth presentation that closes exactly. One suffices.

 **U3 — the E1 puncture.**
 *Definition.* The E1-allowed set T = {(2J, 2J′) : |2J − 2J′| ≤ 2} is closed under componentwise max
 and min. T ∖ {(0,0)}, the set with the physically forbidden J = 0 ↛ 0 transition removed, fails
 meet-closure by exactly four pairs, and all four meets produce (0,0).
 *Searched.* Not found. Selection rules are universally known; their closure properties are not a
 subject these searches reached.
 *Test.* Recompute at caps beyond 20 and confirm the count stays four — done to 20 here. Then repeat
 for M1 (|ΔJ| ≤ 1, no parity change) and E2 (|ΔJ| ≤ 2 with J + J′ ≥ 2): do their allowed sets close,
 and does each forbidden cell cost a constant number of meets?
 *Falsifier.* A cap at which the count is not four, or a second cell produced by a failing meet.

 **U4 — the join/meet asymmetry of the triangle.**
 *Definition.* T = {(2L, 2S, 2J) : |2L − 2S| ≤ 2J ≤ 2L + 2S} is join-closed and meet-broken. Verified
 at caps 6, 8, 10, 12 with 0 join failures and 2,862 / 12,489 / 40,887 / 110,229 failing meets.
 Imposing the parity congruence breaks join as well.
 *Searched.* Not found.
 *Proved.* A.18 gives it, and the proof corrects the guess that preceded it. Joins are closed

 Chapter 15 recovers Λ's coordinate order because its constraint graph is a tree. For an index whose
 graph has cycles, the question is open, and the following is what is known.

 Complete under a targeted attack. Fixing one pair of axes jointly and extending one axis at a time
 with backtracking found a valid ordering in 384 of 384 reorderable instances, sampled deliberately by
 solution density rather than at random. No proof; no counterexample.

    The earlier figure of 139 was a random sample. §28.2 says the search is hardest when the solution is
    nearly unique, so the instances were re-drawn to concentrate there — 101 of the 384 sit in the
    lowest density bucket, and none of them failed.

  solution density                                         mean backtracks
  0.00–0.05                                                23.40
  0.05–0.20                                                6.90
  0.20–0.50                                                1.05
  0.50–1.00                                                0.00

### 28.2 What governs the difficulty
 Ten structural invariants were tested against backtracking — dimension, alphabet size, cell count,
 occupancy, join-irreducibles, poset height, poset width, covers, antichain, rank range, over 211
 reorderable instances. The best correlation was 0.31.

 Solution density governs it, at −0.68 in log over the same instances:

| solution fraction | backtrack-free | mean backtracks |
|---|---|---|
| 0.009 – 0.25 | **24%** | 2.9 |
| 0.25 – 0.50 | 47% | 1.0 |
| 0.50 – 1.00 | 82% | 0.2 |
| 1.00 | **100%** | **0.0** |

    The search is hard exactly when the solution is nearly unique.

### 28.2.1 And that list was enumerated once

 An earlier draft concluded from the 0.31 that the difficulty is not structural. That was a
 conclusion about ten invariants, and the list predates the containment forest, overlap components,
 C1P and the interval structure. Re-run over 928 instances with six invariants discovered since:

  invariant                                   corr. with steps            corr. with density
  best of the original ten                    0.31                        —
  overlap pairs                               0.438                       −0.423
  nesting pairs                               0.375                       −0.640
  distinct row supports                       0.606                       −0.883
  log solution density                        −0.628                      —

 predicts the difficulty.

      Structure determines density; density determines difficulty. The earlier reading had the
      second link and called it the whole chain.

### 28.2.2 Which gives §28.3 a parameter
 Search steps against distinct row supports, over 1,480 instances:

  distinct rows                        mean steps                 max         max / d²
  2                                    1.05                       8           2.00
  3                                    2.63                       10          1.11
  4                                    5.41                       36          2.25
  5                                    8.68                       39          1.56

 The ratio does not climb; the log–log slope is 2.29. That is a measured candidate exponent for
 §28.3's complexity question — on five points, with R² between 0.37 and 0.42. Evidence, not a bound.

### 28.2.3 And it is a landscape statement
 E is a potential on the space of orderings and adjacent transposition is a move. Solution density
 is the size of the basin: a rare solution means a longer descent with more places to stall. §28.3.3
 completes this reading.

### 28.3 Reorderability — the law, the procedure, and what is left
 The question this section asked was: given an index whose constraint graph has cycles, can
 its coordinate order be recovered? The answer has a law, a procedure, and a residue, and none of the
 three is where the section began.

### 28.3.1 The object, correctly identified
      ℛ-closure and closure under join and meet are the SAME CONDITION — 1,487 instances,
      zero disagreements, and confirmed on all 475,800 pairs of Λ. So reorderability is: does some
      relabelling of each axis make X a SUBLATTICE of a product of chains?

 That is lattice embedding, and it is the subject of Rival 1973/74, Larson 1998 and Siggers 2016.
 §28.3's original citations — Stahl & Wille, Yannakakis — were correct; a draft withdrew them on the
 grounds that this was an interval problem, and it is not. The withdrawal is withdrawn.

 And the recovered bound of Chapter 15 is Rival's closed family of irreducible intervals. Siggers'
 Lemma 3.5(ii) states φ_ij exactly.

### 28.3.2 The law
 A relabelling decides, for each axis and each pair of values, which comes first. So the problem
 is a constraint system on those decisions, and every constraint is closed under reversing all of

 its own orientations — 3,781 constraints checked, 100%.                           A   function     invariant     under
 complementation depends only on XOR-differences, so:

  arity — the axes on which two        the constraint      cost
  cells differ                         becomes
  2                                    a single XOR        signed-graph 2-colouring — LINEAR
  3                                    two XORs            2-SAT, and all 14 constraints that arise are 2-SAT
                                                           expressible — LINEAR
  ≥4                                   three or more       contains exactly-one-of-three; no Schaefer class covers
                                       XORs                the language

      THE LAW. Reorderability is a constraint system whose arity is the number of axes on
      which two cells differ. At arity ≤ 3 the language is entirely bijunctive, so the problem is
      linear. At arity ≥ 4 it contains 1-in-3-SAT and admits no Schaefer class.

 The procedure is the law read at low arity; the hardness is the same law read at high arity.
 One statement, two regimes, boundary at arity 3 — and since arity is bounded by d and reaches
 it, at d = 3.

 Measured: at d = 2 every constraint has arity 2 at every alphabet size, and 2-colouring plus
 transitivity decides exactly — 300/300 at \|A\| = 3, 300/300 at \|A\| = 4. At d = 3 with binary axes,
 396 of 396.

 Figure 23.1. Left: the fraction of each arity's constraint language that is 2-SAT expressible — 14 of 14 at arity 3, and
 114 of 141 at arity 4. The boundary is exact. Right: the share of constraints by arity as the dimension rises — arity 2
 falls from 0.62 to 0.26 while arity ≥ 4 grows from nothing to 0.38. The tractable part shrinks with d, and the law
 says why.

### 28.3.3 What the interval machinery was
 Chapter-length work went into C1P, monotone endpoints and PQ-trees, and the d = 2
 characterisation is proved there: X is reorderable iff every row is an interval with both endpoints
 monotone, iff no interval nests strictly inside another. Four lemmas, three verified independently —
 2,047, 3,751 and 20,000 instances — with Booth & Lueker's linear PQ-tree construction cited
 for the fourth.

 **The fourth lemma, verified.** The three lemmas above were checked at 2,047, 3,751 and 20,000
 instances; the fourth stood on Booth and Lueker's construction and on nothing of this book's own.
 It is now discharged, and it did not need a linear-time algorithm:

    A set of intervals admits an ordering in which both endpoints are non-decreasing **iff** no
    interval nests strictly inside another. Sort by left endpoint; if a right endpoint then
    decreases, the later interval has the weakly greater left end and the strictly smaller right
    end, so it nests strictly. Conversely a strictly nesting pair admits no such order. ∎

 Verified exhaustively over all 2,354 interval sets of two to four intervals on ground sets of two to
 five points: zero counterexamples. **Strictly** is load-bearing — an interval sharing an endpoint
 with its container does not nest strictly, and reading it as ordinary containment refutes the lemma
 on 1,098 of those 2,354 sets. That reading was tried first here and was wrong, which is the whole
 reason the qualifier is in the statement. Register 247.

      That apparatus is a REPRESENTATION of a 2-colouring. It is correct and it is not the reason d =
      2 is easy. The reason is that two cells in two dimensions differ on at most two axes.

### 28.3.4 The step law
 Growth from the minimal reorderable sets, adding cells, reaches every reorderable set — with
 a step size measured exhaustively across twelve boxes:

  d                     step                      boxes
  2                     1                         eight, all 2-D

  d                     step                      boxes
  3                     2                         three
  4                     4                         one

 The over-cap cases collapse to a single object: the full box. Its largest reorderable proper subset
 has 3·2^(d−2) cells — three quarters — and the removed cells are a subcube. Verified by construction
 at d = 2, 3, 4 and 5, with one-fewer failing at all four.

      step f(d) = 2^(d−2).

 Figure 23.2. Left: the growth step against dimension — 1, 2, 4 measured exhaustively over twelve boxes, and 8 at d = 5
 by the subcube construction, against 2^(d−2). Right: the box against its largest reorderable proper subset — 3, 6, 12, 24
 cells, exactly three quarters at every dimension. Rival's 1973 bound on maximal sublattices is \|K\| ≤ (3/2)\|L\|; the
 Boolean case is tighter.

 And this is Rival's theorem. His 1973 bound is \|K\| ≤ (3/2)\|L\| for a maximal sublattice;
 Chen–Koh–Tan give the interval form; the large sublattices of 2^[r] are catalogued, and the
 maximal ones studied in finite topology. §E.5 records the precedence.

### 28.3.5 The procedure, and its cost
      DECIDE(X). Build the constraint system on orientations. Arity ≤ 3: 2-colour the signed graph
      and check transitivity — linear. Arity ≥ 4: grow from the minimal reorderable sets with step
      2^(d−2), collect signatures, decide by lookup.

 86, converging in nine rounds. And NextClosure enumerates the sublattices with polynomial
 delay — 1,834 sets in 0.12 s — giving 401 signatures against 401 exhaustive.

 Cost: \|YES\| · \|X\|^{2^(d−2)}. Polynomial in \|X\| for fixed d; exponential in d. Fixed-parameter
 tractable, and not polynomial in both.

 For Λ: d = 8, so ∏\|A_i\|! = 11,943,936 — and Λ needs none of it. Its structure is constructed in
 Chapter 7, its embedding is tight, \|J(Λ)\| = 17 = height, width 7 ≤ 8, and by Dilworth and
 Larson the chain decomposition of J(Λ) IS the axis system.

### 28.3.6 The signature, exhaustively verified
 A cell-space invariant whose FORM does not change with d: the multiset of canonical forms of the
 3-subsets of X. O(\|X\|³) structure, 2^d labels — the two factor, where every order-space method
 cost ∏\|A_i\|! and coupled them.

  box                 subsets                                                  classes                    mixed
  2×2×2               all 256                                                  30                         0
  2×2×3               all 4,096                                                210                        0
  2×3×3               all 262,144                                              4,168                      0

 Three complete boxes, 267,000 subsets, no signature containing both answers. After the duality
 merge the 19 canonical forms reduce to 12 with no loss.

### 28.3.7 Three method classes ruled out
 Each with its measurement, and each a result rather than a failure:

 Projection-based criteria. §18.4: closure is a d-dimensional condition and no projection serves as a
 criterion. Thirteen of seventeen attempted criteria were seed-independent invariants — all
 necessary, none sufficient, with the gap widening as nesting deepened.

 Local search through valid orders. The valid set is DISCONNECTED — 1.66 to 2.19 components,
 and the components are orbits of the identical-fibre swap group, exact on 493 of 493. So descent
 plateaus: 89.8%, and 96.7% with bounded uphill moves.

 Forbidden-substructure procedures. Tucker's families are unbounded, so no finite census decides
 — and the census is finite within any box, which is what reopened the question. The infinite antichain
 lives across indices, not in one.

### 28.3.8 The residue
 The language is NP-complete — it contains exactly-one-of-three and no Schaefer class covers it, with
 the smallest obstruction exhibited on three XOR variables.

 The realisability is blocked. Three reduction attempts, all over-constraining in the same direction:
 satisfiable formulas encoding as non-reorderable, never the reverse. The map X → C(X) is global,
 non-separable and non-monotone, so it admits no local editing.

 And the restriction is not exploitable by sparsity — the constraint hypergraph has d vertices and up
 to 2^d − 1 hyperedges. It is complete, so treewidth gives back the 2^d bound already known.

    Three walls: hardness blocked at realisability, tractability blocked at the completeness of
    the hypergraph, and the FPT bound between them as the best known.

### 28.3.9 And it is not this book's problem
 Λ's constraint graph is a tree. Its nine recovered extra edges are implied. Every sublattice and
 interval of Λ has E = 0. Its own case is decidable by enumeration, and it arrives with a
 derivation — box → interval → sublattice → product, three preserving rules, no search.

    The open problem concerns cell sets arriving with no construction. This book never has
    one.

 §E.6 records that the complexity question may already be settled in Ryter & Schmid 1994 or
 Adams–Dwinger–Schmid 1996, both unread.

### 28.4 The lists this work enumerated once
 The target list for the novelty search was audited by closing the relation set, and it was
 incomplete. From {V = 4ν/3h, λ² = (2/3)T, w·V = 8λ², T = Z²R/ν²} the closure yields w/T = 4(h/ν), e/T =
 3(h/ν)², and bits(estimate) ≈ 2·bits(bracket) + constant — none of them on the list.

    That is Chapter 6's defect committed by the searcher rather than by a chemist — a
    structure admitting cells its keeper never enumerated.

### 28.4.1 And the audit itself was run once
 The relation set has grown since. Closing the eight polynomial relations the book now states gives a
 Gröbner basis of 18 where the original four gave 6, and seven further relations reduce to zero that
 did not before — including V·e = w, w² = (16/3)·T·e and T·h² = eν²/3.

 Worse, the closure is over polynomial relations only. The book now states at least nine that are not:
 A^m(x^p) = (−1)^m x^p/(p−1)^m, V = 2/tanh(kh/2), self-concordance, the modular rank law,

 Σ_q\|A_q\|·\|B_q\| = \|Λ\|, F(−1) = 2, E(X) as non-pairwise content, and the reorderability theorem. None
 was ever audited against any list.

    E(target list) is not 3. It was 3 for the relation set of one moment.

### 28.4.2 Which is a defect of five lists, not one
 This chapter contains five enumerations, and every one was made once:

  the list                                    what it omitted
  §28.4's search targets                      7 polynomial relations, 9 non-polynomial
  §28.2's structural invariants               six, one of which beats its stated best twofold
  §29.1's celestial objects                   six the method plainly admits
  §29.2's string objects                      five, two of them measured in this work
  §29.3's statistic                           stated against the wrong denominator

 §2.10 reads enumerate targets before searching. It should read enumerate before searching, and
 re-enumerate whenever the set grows — which is this section's own content, applied to itself.

## 29. The method outside spectroscopy
 The method was built on one index and tested on one collection. If it is a method rather than a
 description, it must apply where neither was available. This chapter runs it on four subjects it
 was not built for.

### 29.1 Celestial mechanics and the nucleus
 Objects tested against the index, none of them in the collection. A method that transfers is a
 different claim from one that fits.

### 29.1.1 Celestial mechanics — families, not trajectories
 What does not transfer. Sensitive dependence destroys monotonicity along a chaotic trajectory.
 Nothing here touches Poincaré.

  tested                                   result
  Lagrange L1, L2, L3 in μ (Euler's        monotone, convex, 3-monotone; 18 of 18 containments at orders 1–3
  collinear solutions)
  the same at order 3                      widths 6.9 × 10⁻⁴ (L1), 3.6 × 10⁻⁹ (L3)
  Hill stability of hierarchical triples   monotone and convex in the mass ratio; V ≈ 100
  (Mardling & Aarseth)
  Hill radius (μ/3)^{1/3}                  monotone, convex, 3-monotone; V = 47.9
  Roche limit ∝ ρ^{−1/3}                   monotone, convex, 3-monotone; V = 17.9
  planetary semi-major axes                monotone, not convex — the third difference changes sign between
                                           Jupiter and Saturn, where Titius–Bode fails worst
  mean-motion resonances                   §16.7.1: E(X) recovers the order cut at 7/8 from occupancy alone
  satellite counts vs Hill radius          log–log +0.86 across six planets — §21.14.1's capacity bound

 The pole appears at the first point one looks. At μ = 0.030 with a step of h = 0.010, V is 24.6 at
 L1, 12.4 at L2 and 16,423 at L3 — the last because L3 moves almost linearly in μ. L4 and L5 sit on it
 exactly: (1/2 − μ, ±√3/2), the first linear and the second constant.

    Which corrects §18.5. The pole is where a bracket becomes unnecessary, not worthless — a
    vanishing second difference makes linear interpolation exact.

 And one object the method cannot touch. L4/L5 are linearly stable for μ < 0.0385209; Earth–Moon
 and Sun–Jupiter both qualify. That is a threshold, not a family — a single number, with nothing for
 a bracket to act on. The method applies to sequences and is silent on thresholds.

 Signs must be read from the data. L1 and L3 alternate −, +, −, +; L2 alternates +, −, +, −, and
 assuming the Rydberg pattern produces bounds that cross.

### 29.1.2 The nucleus — a second index of the same construction
 An atom's mass sits in its nucleus, and nucleons are fermions. Indexed by (N, L, 2j, occupancy)
 with occ ≤ 2j+1, the shell model is closed under join and meet with E(X) = 0, and shell-order filling
 gives 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82.

    Λ gives chemistry. The nucleon index gives mass. This book indexes one of them; Z is a label
    on a channel, never a coordinate.

### 29.2 String theory — the pole, the generating function, and a
 disanalogy
### 29.2.1 Three objects on the pole
 α′m² = N − 1 has second difference zero. So do two more:

  object                                   form                                  V
  string mass spectrum                     m² linear in N                        infinite
  Regge trajectory                         J = α′m² + α₀                         infinite
  central charge                           c=D                                   infinite

 All three join L4 and L5. A bracket is unnecessary on any of them: two levels determine every other,
 exactly.

### 29.2.2 The degeneracy is where the content is
 log d(N) is monotone, convex and 3-monotone, with V ≈ 147 at N ≈ 14 — an ordinary bracketable
 channel, steeper than a Rydberg series.

### 29.2.3 The partition function is Λ's expression with counts
 ∏(1 − q^n)^{−24} has counts where Chapter 11's F has booleans. An index, and an index with
 multiplicity. Both close, for dual reasons: the string's modes are independent; Λ's coordinates couple
 only along a tree. §11.7's three conditions have independence as their degenerate case.

### 29.2.4 No critical dimension, and a ladder
 Λ closes at every dimension 2–8 with E = 0. D = 26 falls out of anomaly cancellation; Λ's 8 is a
 modelling choice.

 And each Λ_d is the exact projection of Λ_{d+1}, closure preserved both ways, with fibres of 1 to 4
 preimages — the extra coordinate carries real information. That is the relation M-theory's eleventh
 dimension has to the ten-dimensional string. What is missing is any reason for the ladder to stop.

### 29.2.5 And no Hagedorn point, for a stated reason
 d(N) ~ exp(4π√N) diverges above a limiting temperature. Λ's rank sequence is finite and
 log-concave, peak 122 at rank 11.

    Capped coordinates give a finite index and a Sperner bound. Uncapped modes give
    exponential degeneracy and a limiting temperature. Λ's finiteness is what capping buys.

### 29.3 The Calabi–Yau catalogue

### 29.3.1 Self-duality, measured
 Batyrev's polar duality swaps the Hodge numbers and the Kreuzer–Skarke list is complete
 over reflexive 4-polytopes — 473,800,776 of them, 30,108 distinct pairs. So the set is closed under
 the involution by construction, and three published counts measure it:

    248,305 with h¹¹ ≥ 140 · 248,305 with h²¹ ≥ 140 · 495,515 with at least one · and 248,305 +
    248,305 − 495,515 = 1,095, as reported.

                                                                 Λ                       KS
  self-dual cells                                                8 of 976                all
  rank polynomial palindromic                                    false                   true

### 29.3.2 The thin tip is a defect of the construction
 h¹¹ + h²¹ < 22 is sparse in the KS list and populated by complete intersections, Klemm–Kreuzer toric
 CICYs and conifold transitions. By §16.7.1's test the absence is removable — not by
 re-coordinatising but by re-constructing — so it is a defect of the index, like the periodic table's 36
 and unlike the belt's six.

### 29.3.3 The Pareto strength, against the right denominator
 1,095 of the 495,515 polytopes with one large Hodge number have both: 0.221%. Stated
 against the full 473.8 million it reads 0.0002%, a factor of 956 — true and uninformative, because the
 denominator includes polytopes with no large Hodge number at all.

    §12.8.1 finds the same trade inside Λ: \|A_q\| falls as \|B_q\| rises. A catalogue with a bounded
    coordinate difference and a large total must be Pareto-shaped, and 0.221% is how strongly.

### 29.3.4 E(X) on a specifiable slice, and 540 predictions
 The 30,108 pairs are a gzipped file this session could not read. But one slice of the catalogue is
 specified exactly in print, and a slice is enough for the operator.

 Candelas, de la Ossa, He & Szendroi (Triadophilia, ATMP 12 (2008) 429) state that the KS list's χ = ±6
 points have Hodge numbers (h, h+3) and (h+3, h) for 13 ≤ h ≤ 128, and name the exclusions: h = 102,
 103, 115, 117 and 119–126. That is a complete cell set — 208 cells — and ℛ applies to it.

    E(X) = 540. 498 join failures and 498 meet failures of 21,528 pairs.

 Chapter 6 reads E(X) > 0 as what a structure admits and lacks. The periodic table admits 36 such
 cells and they are the elements. Here the slice admits 540 and they are Hodge pairs the
 catalogue must contain if the pair set is closed.

 The slice cannot contain them, and the reason is geometric. Two parallel lines have no fixed point:
 the join of (h, h+3) and (h+3, h) is (h+3, h+3). So ℛ immediately names the diagonal.

  the predictions
  cells                                     540
  distinct χ values                         5 — only 0, ±2, ±4
  on the diagonal, χ = 0                    112, from (13,13) to (131,131)
  h¹¹ + h²¹ range                           26 to 262

 The slice was cut at χ = ±6 and the closure predicts inward. It says the set the slice came from fills
 the gap between the two lines — which is where the rest of the Kreuzer–Skarke list lives.

 24.3.4.2 The fourth falsification test, run

 The file is missing, so the predictions cannot be looked up. They can still be refuted, because
 the literature states where the catalogue's contents lie.

  test                                                                     result
  h¹¹ ≥ 1 and h²¹ ≥ 1                                                      540 / 540
  h¹¹ + h²¹ ≤ 502, the published maximum                                   540 / 540
  mirror partner present                                                   540 / 540
  falling where Candelas et al. record "essentially every site occupied"   540 / 540
  falling in the "thinly populated" tip, where a prediction would be       0 / 540
  refuted
  falsified                                                                0
  individually named in print                                              X₁₉,₁₉ (split bicubic), X₂₀,₂₀ (the 24-cell)

    Zero falsifications, two named confirmations, and every prediction inside the region
    published as fully populated.

 This is weaker than a lookup and it is not nothing. A prediction landing in the sparse tip would have
 been refuted, and none does. The test is against the literature's characterisation of the file
 rather than against the file.

 24.3.4.3 And the void reads the same way

                                                                                    cells        predictions
  all h from 13 to 128                                                              232          589
  with the documented exclusions                                                    208          540

 The 24 excluded values — 102, 103, 115, 117 and the run 119–126 — reduce the predictions by
 49. The gaps in the published list are not noise with respect to closure: removing them moves the set
 toward its own normal form, which is what §5 says a void should do when it is structural rather than
 accidental.

 What remains of item D is the lookup. 540 named cells, a file, and an afternoon.

 four decline modes each have a worked case; and the parked questions of earlier drafts — C₆ density,
 antiprotonic helium, the isoelectronic law — are resolved in Chapters 15 and 17. What remains open is
 enumerated and closed as an index in Appendix E: eight items, not one of which blocks a
