   174	```python
   175	from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph
   176	from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet
   177	
   178	styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
   179

   182	
   183	# Superscripts: use <super> tag
   184	squared = Paragraph("x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>", styles['Normal'])

Rendered: **20 pages, A4, searchable, 922 KB.** XeLaTeX via pandoc with FreeSerif, table of contents with PDF bookmarks, running heads.

Audit 5 run on the built artefact, not the source:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| missing characters | **0** |
| fonts embedded / subsetted / with unicode maps | **8 of 8** |
| text layer | 59,392 characters extractable |
| search probes — `199,130`, `41,682`, `736,918`… | all hit; `g ≤ q ≤ k` returns 5 |
| replacement or box characters | **0** |
| figures embedded, effective resolution | 8, at **300–353 ppi** |
| lines extending past the text frame | **0 of 20 pages** |

**The render found a defect my own glyph audit had passed, and it is register 190's shape exactly.** I checked all 46 non-ASCII codepoints against the installed fonts and reported full coverage — but I tested the *regular* face, and the document sets ⅅ in **bold**. FreeSerif Bold does not carry U+2145. XeLaTeX reported it, and the fix is a declared fallback to DejaVu Sans, which carries both letterlike symbols in regular, bold and oblique. An audit that reads the wrong artefact will pass anything, and mine did.

Two smaller notes. I deleted the previous PDF before re-rendering, because a failed build leaves the old file in place and reading it would have reported 20 clean pages from an artefact that was never rebuilt — the same trap in miniature. And one probe flagged ν as absent from the text layer; localised before recording, per §4.7, it is absent from the *source* — the paper never uses it. Not a defect, and worth the thirty seconds it took to establish rather than logging it.

The figures land at 300–353 ppi against the book's inherited median of 164, so that class is closed for this material.

"""The twenty prime audits of The Method 1.3 §3, run against
On the Matter of Time Travel. Exits with the number of failures.
Every audit prints its evidence, not merely its verdict."""
import re, os, subprocess, unicodedata, sys
from itertools import combinations, product

SRC = "paper.md"
PDF = "On_the_Matter_of_Time_Travel.pdf"
FIGDIR = "fig"
S = open(SRC, encoding="utf-8").read()
TXT = subprocess.run(["pdftotext", PDF, "-"], capture_output=True,
                     text=True, encoding="utf-8").stdout

results = []
def rec(n, name, ok, note):
    results.append((n, name, ok, note))
    print(f"{n:>2}  {name:<12} {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {note}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 1 LATTICE
def lam(NM,EM,LM,KM,FM,extra=0):
    out=[]
    for n in range(1,NM+1):
     for l in range(0,min(LM,n-1)+1):
      for k in range(1,min(KM,2*(2*l+1))+1):
       for q in range(0,k+1):
        for s in range(0,k+1):
         for e in range(1,EM+1):
          for f in range(0,min(FM,e-1)+1):
           for g in range(0,min(q,2*(2*f+1))+1):
            out.append((n,l,k,q,e,f,g,s))
    return out
L8 = lam(3,3,1,3,1)
SET = set(L8)
jm = sum(1 for a,b in combinations(L8,2)
         if tuple(map(max,a,b)) not in SET or tuple(map(min,a,b)) not in SET)

    f"listed-and-uncited {sorted(uncited)} · cited-and-unlisted {sorted(unlisted)}")

L10 = [c+(v,) for c in L9 for v in range(c[8], c[6]+1)]
arith = (len(L8)==tower[8] and len(L9)==tower[9] and len(L10)==tower[10])
# and one digit altered must break it, per 4.6
canfail = (len(L8) != 977)
rec(14,"ARITHMETIC", arith and canfail,
    f"Λ₈={len(L8)} Λ₉={len(L9)} Λ₁₀={len(L10)} rebuilt from §7.1 · shown able to fail: {canfail}")

enum.append(("Appendix B.1 lists eight", len(re.findall(r'^\| [1-8] \|', S, re.M))==8,
             str(len(re.findall(r'^\| [1-8] \|', S, re.M)))))
enum.append(("Part VI: register entries", n_reg==stated, f"{n_reg} vs stated {stated}"))
oc = re.findall(r'\*\*O(\d)', S)
enum.append(("Appendix C items O1..On contiguous", oc==[str(i+1) for i in range(len(oc))], ",".join(oc)))
badenum=[e for e in enum if not e[1]]
rec(15,"ENUMERATION", not badenum,
    " · ".join(f"{n}: {v}" for n,_,v in enum))

secnums = [int(m) for m in re.findall(r'^## (\d+)\. ', S, re.M)]
gaps = [i for i in range(1,len(secnums)) if secnums[i] != secnums[i-1]+1]

rec(19,"SEQUENCE", not gaps and not dup,
    f"§1–§{max(secnums)} present, {len(secnums)} sections, "
    f"{len(gaps)} breaks in ascent, duplicates: {dup}")

    f"10 source strings probed in the artefact's text layer · {len(fid)} absent {fid}")

seen_part = False
for line in S.split("\n"):
    if re.match(r'^# PART|^# APPENDICES|^# On the Matter', line): seen_part = True
    if re.match(r'^## \d+\. ', line) and not seen_part: orphan.append(line[:40])

print("§3 names seven; §3.8 adds DEPTH, SEQUENCE, PROJECTION; the registers add")
print("ARITHMETIC (14), ENUMERATION (15), FIDELITY, SCOPE, ANTECEDENT — fifteen in all.")

print("not as passing: an assertion is not an enumeration (§E.4.1).")

content.thinking:
I'm identifying a real defect in the attribution section — seven works were listed but never actually cited in the text, including entries from Birkhoff, Dilworth, Nesterov, Nemirovskii, Racah, Rival, and Siggers. The issue with Pixley and Tarski turned out to be an extraction error where my tool only captured first surnames, so they appeared as unlisted when they were actually referenced as secondary authors in the bibliography.

The fix requires citing Birkhoff properly since the down-set correspondence appears in the paper, while removing the other five entries entirely since they belong to a different work's bibliography, not this one. I'm also correcting two detector artifacts: the enumeration check was counting rows across the entire document instead of just Appendix B.1, and the projection check failed because pandoc converted straight quotes to smart quotes in the PDF, which I need to normalize before comparison. For the scope audit, I'm finding that 17 out of 53 percentage claims were flagged as issues.

Most of these flagged claims are actually detector artifacts—table rows where the cap appears in an adjacent column and my backward search window missed the header. But a few are genuine: the reachability figures in §8 for Λ₉ are stated without indicating which caps they're measured at, and the same applies to a quoted figure from §12.11.5. One flagged percentage (21.3%) is just a word-count ratio where no cap applies, so that's an artifact. The real finding here is that §8's reachability figures need a single sentence clarifying which caps they correspond to.

Now I'll update the paper with the proper attribution and cap statement in §8, clean up those two artifact checks, and run the analysis again.

content.thinking:
All nine figures are Λ₉/Λ₁₂ at book caps. The repair I made in §8 added a cap statement to the prose, but the percentages tell different stories — 21.3% is purely a word-count ratio with no cap involved, while 11.4%, 24.7%, and 0.4% appear in §8's table and Figure 3 caption, though my added prose statement comes after the table so the backward-looking check doesn't catch it for those table entries.

The 3.5% figure is quoted directly from the book at its stated caps, genuinely uncapped in this paper, and the §9 mention has no cap either. The detector is actually measuring something real — these are cap-dependent figures whose cap statement isn't within reach. The cleanest solution is to make the cap statement global in Part 0 rather than local, add the cap to Figure 3's caption and the §9 mention and the 3.5% references, then re-run. If 21.3% persists as a genuine artefact, I should record it as such rather than suppress it by loosening the check.

The real issue is that 21.3% isn't actually cap-dependent — it's a word-count ratio, not a percentage-of-cells claim. So the check should scope itself to exclude that kind of quantity, which is a legitimate refinement of the detector's purpose, not a loosening. I'll fix the eight real issues and adjust the check's context test to accept "words" and "ratio" contexts, then re-run and annotate the remaining finding.

**Fifteen run, fifteen pass, five unrunnable.** Exit code 0. The suite is a file — `OMTT_audits.py` — so a build that has not been audited cannot be mistaken for one that has, per §3.9.

**The set had to be recovered before it could be run.** *The Method 1.3* never lists the twenty in one place. §3 names seven; §3.8 adds DEPTH, SEQUENCE and PROJECTION; the registers add ARITHMETIC, ENUMERATION, FIDELITY, SCOPE and ANTECEDENT — fifteen. **Audits 8–13 and 16–18 exist only as a count.** They are recorded as unrunnable rather than passing, on §E.4.1's own ruling that an assertion is not an enumeration — the ruling the book applied to Q and never applied to its audits. That is register entry 11 and it is a finding about the book, not this paper.

**Three defects in the paper, found and repaired.**

**ATTRIBUTION** was the real one, and it is the failure the book calls *dishonest* rather than wrong. Six works sat in the reference list and were never cited: Birkhoff, Dilworth, Nesterov and Nemirovskii, Racah, Rival, Siggers — carried over from *The Method*'s bibliography into a paper that does not use them, implying a use that was not made. Birkhoff is now cited where the down-set correspondence is used; the other five are gone.

**SCOPE** caught eleven cap-dependent figures whose caps were out of reach — the reachability proportions, the overlap, the 3.5% quoted from §12.11.5. Register 292's shape. Now stated globally in Part 0 and locally at each.

**ENCODING**, from the earlier turn, already in the register.

**And the instruments needed more repair than the paper: five against three.** ENUMERATION counted table rows across the whole document instead of one appendix. PROJECTION compared a straight apostrophe against pandoc's typographic one. SCOPE's own count was a broken regex. Then writing Appendix B.2 broke two more — a number-word list with no entry for *eleven*, and a section boundary that swallowed the new table.

Every instrument fault was one mechanism: **a literal narrowing a check to the cases foreseen when it was written.** Registers 305, 310 and 337 record the identical thing three times in the book. Five more here is the strongest evidence in the paper that it is a mechanism and not anecdote — and it is why four of the six flags this run produced were the detectors and not the paper, which is the ratio §3.9 reports.

The register now stands at **eleven entries**, and the run is printed at Appendix B.2 with its evidence column, so a reader can re-run it rather than take the verdict.

**What §16 actually establishes.** "A closed index contains its own contradiction" is the heading of the self-defence chapter, and the content is three disjoint mechanisms: ℛ(Λ) = Λ catches rules not recoverable from cells; ⅅ ≥ 1 catches a wrong value in data or derivation; χ total catches a missing value coerced to a real one. Each was demonstrated on a real error. The chapter's conclusion is not that the index harbours a contradiction — it is that **the index will surface one if it is there**, and §16.7.2 immediately limits it: a coherent fabrication has no missing cells, is full, satisfies every law in the book, and contains 75 configurations no atom can have. Self-consistency detects an isolated error and *certifies* a systematic one.

So "contains its own contradiction" means *carries the means of finding one*. It does not mean the index holds a live inconsistency, and §30.4.1 is emphatic in the other direction: with no negation in the language, **a contradiction cannot be written at all**. The fixed point sits where the paradox would have been. Those two are the same chapter's two halves, and the second is what makes the temporal structure safe.

**Where I think the real connection is, and it is not that one.** The thing in this session that behaves like a contradiction living inside the object is §12.11.6, and it is exact: the E1 selection rule is a closed index; remove the one cell nature forbids, J = 0 ↛ 0, and closure fails by exactly four meets — and **all four failing meets produce the removed cell**. The index restores the thing you deleted. Generalised at §16.8.4: deletion is always repaired, exhaustively 976 of 976 in this paper's §9, with the criterion that no cell uniquely witnesses a value or an envelope maximum.

That is a self-healing structure with a proof and a count, and it is the nearest thing in the framework to Novikov self-consistency. But note carefully what it is not: it is a statement about **deletion**, not about causation. Nothing in it says a timeline resists alteration. It says a closed index resists having a cell taken out of it, because the remaining cells still imply it.

Zero violations at six of seven stages, and the single violation is at Λ₉′ — the one stage the book itself flags as broken.

> **The law.** At a cut of the constraint graph on coordinate v, each surviving component **shrinks** if it contains a parent of v, **grows** if it contains a child of v, and is flat if it contains neither. Raising v raises the floor on its parents and the ceiling on its children.

**89 component tests across seven stages and every cut: one violation.** And it is at Λ₉′, whose constraint graph is the only one in the tower with a **cycle** — f–g–2S′, the tightening the book prices at 93 cells and describes as *the tree or the tightness*. The law is a theorem about trees, and it fails at exactly the stage that stopped being one.

**The Pauli coupling, defined at every stage.**

| stage | two-parent coordinate | its parents | cut behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Λ₈ | **g** | f, q | **all components shrink** — no opposition |
| Λ₉ | g | f, q | opposed — g has gained a child, 2S′ |
| Λ₉′ | g **and 2S′** | f,q · g,f | law violated — the cycle |
| Λ₁₀ | g | f, q | opposed |
| Λ₁₁ | g | f, q | opposed |
| Λ₁₂ | g | f, q | opposed |
| Λ₁₃ | g | f, q | opposed |

**g ≤ min(q, 4f+2) is the unique two-parent bound in the entire tower as built.** Every coordinate from the ninth axis to the thirteenth enters with exactly one parent, which is why closure survives thirteen dimensions and forty-seven million ambient cells. §11.5 calls it *the one coupling, and it is the Pauli principle*; the tower confirms that it is not merely the one coupling of Λ₈ but the one coupling of all of it.

**And the two places a second could have entered are the two places the book records a price.** Λ₉′ adds 2S′ ≤ 2f+1 and makes 2S′ two-parent — 93 cells bought, the tree lost, and the only violation of the law in the whole run. Λ₁₂'s law for K is 2K ≤ 2J_c + 2f with the cell's own f — two parents — and §12.11.3.1 records the book substituting f_max, the cap, to keep one parent and the cylinder, at 2,475 cells.

**Now the correction to what I said last turn.** I claimed opposition fails at two-parent coordinates. That is wrong, and the run shows why: at Λ₈, g has two parents **and no child**, so every component holds a parent and every one shrinks. From Λ₉ onward g has the child 2S′, and opposition returns. So the failure was never about two parents — it was about **g being a leaf on the child side**. The Pauli coupling is distinguished by having two parents; the *absence of opposition* is a separate and temporary fact about Λ₈ that the ninth axis repairs.

I had the right exception and the wrong reason for it, which is the third prediction I have got wrong this session — and, as with the other two, the correction is worth more than the prediction was.

chat_messages.text:
Same place as three turns ago, and I'd rather say that plainly than dress up the last three turns as progress toward it.

The K work was real and it was not about time. It found a probable error in the book — the tight K costs 15,150 cells at Λ₁₂ and 45,450 at Λ₁₃, not 2,475 — and it found that the price of keeping the tree grows with f_max. Both worth having. Neither touches the antecedent.

**What has actually accumulated on time, across fourteen turns.** One law: g ≤ q ≤ k makes occupancy a global clock, cycles live only in its level sets, every step of a cycle is conservative. Proved, cap-free, shown able to fail. Around it, a body of measurement — the three eras, the Markov property, the future as a saturated interval, the pushback floor of 16, the step law, the groupoid at 389 cells where the forward and reversed indices agree. That is a coherent and I think genuinely good account of **how time behaves if it is an index of transitions**.

**And the gap has not moved once.** Every result is conditional on that *if*. §16.7.3 is the obstacle and it is not rhetorical: a complete consistent index of a city that does not exist certifies itself perfectly, and only going there distinguishes it. Going there means a measurement the composition order predicts and something else does not. E(Λ) = 0 says the index has none to offer — that is §18.6's whole content, the prediction budget is the closure defect and ours is zero.

**What I think is worth saying about the pattern of these turns.** Every time we return to the question, the productive move has been to take some structure and compute it, and each computation has been about the *index*. That is not a failure of aim. It is P20 operating: the question *is time such an index* is posed in the documentary language, which has no closure mechanism, so no amount of work inside the index closes it in either direction. §27.1 proves the same thing for novelty and the book's response there is the one I'd take here — name it, state what a search or a measurement could settle, and stop arguing.

**So the honest options, and they are three.**

Accept the conditional result and publish it as conditional. The paper already does; Part II is stated as theorems about indices and §11 says so explicitly.

Or find the measurement. That is the only thing that would move it, and it would have to come from outside — a physical system where composition order and something else disagree. I have no candidate and I would be inventing one if I offered it.

Or take what the session actually produced and finish it. The paper is six turns stale, the precedent searches on the occupancy clock and the step law have never been run, and there is now a probable defect in *The Method 1.3* at §12.11.5 that deserves its own entry with the four routes attached.

I'd take the third, and I'd stop calling it time travel in the write-up. What we have is a clock, an arrow, a reversible core and a proof that nothing can be removed — under a stated hypothesis about what the cells are. That is a stronger paper than one that claims the hypothesis.

## 4.3. Weighted systems

Weighted systems are transition systems whose transitions are given weights drawn from a semiring where addition and multiplication characterise transition branching and chaining thus offering a modular approach to model several quantitative aspects as shown e.g. in [25, 32]

Let us recall some preliminary definitions. A semiring $(W,+,0,\cdot,1)$ is said to be positively ordered whenever its carrier W admits a partial order $(W,\leq)$ such that the unit 0 is the bottom element of this ordering and semiring operations are monotonic in both components i.e.: $x \leq y$ implies $x \diamond z \leq y \diamond z$ and $z \diamond x \leq z \diamond y$ for $\phi \in \{+,\cdot\}$ and $x,y,z \in W$ . A semiring is positively ordered if and only if it is zerosumfree i.e. x+y=0 implies x=y=0; the natural order $x \triangleleft y \iff \exists z.x+z=y$ is the weakest one rendering W positively ordered.

The semiring constructed in Theorem 5.10 actually has the structure of a graded semiring. Although a graded structure is usually defined for rings [Lan02], we apply it to semirings. A graded semiring $\langle D, \oplus, \times, 1, 0 \rangle$ over $\mathcal{M}$ is a semiring where $D = \biguplus_{m \in \mathcal{M}} D_m$ , $D_m$ is a commutative monoid, and $D_m D_{m'} \subseteq D_{mm'}$ for all $m, m' \in \mathcal{M}$ . It is clear that the semiring in Theorem 5.10 is a graded semiring over $\mathcal{M}_{\Gamma} \cup \{\bot\}$ where $D = \biguplus_{\sigma \in \mathcal{M}_{\Gamma}} D'_{\sigma} \uplus D'_{\bot}$ , $D'_{\sigma} = \{\langle \sigma, a \rangle \mid a \in D_{\sigma}\}$ , and $D'_{\bot} = \{\bot\}$ . Furthermore, $D'_{\sigma}$ has no infinite ascending chains on $\Box$ if the indexed semiring is locally bounded. Thus, it is also possible to present our framework based on graded semirings.

# 6. SIMPLIFIED STRUCTURE: MULTIPLICATION ON STRICTLY COMPATIBLE SIGNATURES



An indexed semiring has a multiplication indexed by two stack signatures. However, it is often simpler to consider and implement a restricted multiplication defined only for strictly compatible signatures. We show that an indexed semiring over the ordered monoid of stack signatures can be constructed from such a structure.

We introduce weight structures that have a restricted multiplication $\odot_{\sigma_1,\sigma_2}$ for strictly compatible $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ .

**Definition 6.1.** A weight structure W over a stack alphabet $\Gamma$ is $\langle \{D_{\sigma}\}, \{\oplus_{\sigma}\}, \{\odot_{\sigma_1, \sigma_2}\}, \{0_{\sigma}\}, \{1_{\sigma}\}, \{\uparrow_{\sigma, \sigma'}\} \rangle$ such that

- $D_{\sigma}$ is a set for each proper stack signature $\sigma$ .
- $\langle D_{\sigma}, \oplus_{\sigma}, 0_{\sigma} \rangle$ is a commutative monoid for each proper stack signature $\sigma$ .

# 4.2 Distributivity and maximal vs. prime ideals in conjunctive join-semilattices

We have shown that in a distributive join semilattice, all maximal ideals are prime. Suppose L is a conjunctive join semilattice that is not distributive. Does L have a maximal ideal that is not prime? In this subsection, we answer in the affirmative for complete (and in particular, for finite) join semilattices.

Let L be a finite conjunctive join semilattice. We can represent L as a $T_1$ subbase on a finite set X. Spec<sub>Max</sub> L is identified with X in the discrete topology. Each point $x \in X$ is identified with the maximal ideal $m_x := \{ a \in L \mid x \notin a \}$ .

Suppose L fails to be distributive. Then there are $a,b,c\in L$ such that: $a\subseteq b\cup c$ and

$$\forall b', c' \in L, \ b' \subseteq a \cap b \& c' \subseteq a \cap c \ \Rightarrow \ b' \cup c' \neq a.$$

#### 3. General Observations

In this section we note observations about complements of maximal sublattices in general, independent of restrictions we have on the initial lattice $\mathcal{L}$ . Some of these observations give partial answers to [15, Question 3]:

**Question 3.** Suppose P is a finite ordered set occurring as a suborder of a finite lattice. Is there a finite lattice $\mathcal{L}$ and a maximal sublattice $\mathcal{M}$ of $\mathcal{L}$ such that $P \cong \mathcal{L} \setminus \mathcal{M}$ ? How can such ordered sets be characterized?

**Observation 3.1.** The complement of a maximal sublattice of any lattice will be contained entirely within an indecomposable component of that lattice. 

In particular, if x is comparable to every element of $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{S}$ is a sublattice of $\mathcal{L}$ , then both $\mathcal{S} \cup \uparrow x$ and $\mathcal{S} \cup \downarrow x$ are sublattices of $\mathcal{L}$ and hence if $\mathcal{S}$ is maximal, its complement must be entirely contained in either $\uparrow x$ or $\downarrow x$ .

*Proof.* Let S be a sublattice of $\mathcal{L}$ . We show that $S \cup \downarrow x$ is a sublattice of $\mathcal{L}$ . Fix $u, v \in S \cup \downarrow x$ . If both u and v are in S, then $u \lor v \in S$ and $u \land v \in S$ . If both u and v are in $\downarrow x$ , then $u \lor v \in \downarrow x$ and $u \land v \in \downarrow x$ . Suppose $u \in S \setminus \downarrow x$ and $v \in \downarrow x$ . Then $u \in \uparrow x$ since x is comparable to everything and so $v \leq x \leq u$ . That is, $u \land v = v \in \downarrow x$ and $u \lor v = u \in S$ . 

In all cases, $u \lor v \in S \cup \uparrow x$ and $u \land v \in S \cup \uparrow x$ and thus $S \cup \uparrow x$ is a sublattice of $\mathcal{L}$ . An analogous argument shows that $S \cup \uparrow x$ is a sublattice of $\mathcal{L}$ .

content.title: (PDF) Primes, irreducibles and extremal lattices
content.text:
These elements can be used to characterize certain types of lattices. For example, a lattice is distributive if and only if every join-irreducible is coprime. Similarly, a lattice is meet-pseudocomplemented if and only if each atom is coprime.

This paper studies certain types of join and meet-irreducibles called coprimes and primes. These elements can be used to characterize certain types of lattices. For example, a lattice is distributive if and only if every join-irreducible is coprime. Similarly, a lattice is meet-pseudocomplemented if and only if each atom is coprime. Furthermore, these elements naturally decompose lattices into sublattices so that often properties of the original lattice can be deduced from properties of the sublattice. Not every lattice has primes and coprimes. This paper shows that lattices which are “long enough” must have primes and coprimes and that these elements and the resulting decompositions can be used to study such lattices. 

The length of every finite lattice is bounded above by the minimum of the number of meet-irreducibles (meet-rank) and the number of join-irreducibles (join-rank) that it has.

An equivalent characterization of left modular lattices is obtained in terms of edge-labellings, together with necessary and sufficient conditions on the doubling steps in the construction of congruence normal lattices that ensure left modularity or extremality. We prove that a congruence uniform lattice is shellable if and only if it is extremal. We answer a question of Barnard by constructing a counterexample showing that an induced subcomplex of a canonical join complex need not itself be such a complex. Finally, we show that the order dimension of a semidistributive extremal lattice equals the chromatic number of the complement of its Galois graph, generalizing a theorem of Dilworth for distributive lattices.

cd /home/claude && python3 - <<'PY'
S=open('paper.md',encoding='utf-8').read()

# ---- 1. demote the occupancy clock in the abstract and §6 ----
S=S.replace(
"**Two.** Λ₉'s composition law is shown to carry a **global time function**, and the result is promoted from an extent bound to a law. In any index whose cells are transitions subject to g ≤ q ≤ k, occupancy is non-increasing along composition; closed timelike curves exist exactly within its level sets; and every step of one is conservative. The proof is one line, uses no caps, and is demonstrated capable of failing.",
"**Two.** Λ₉'s composition law is shown to carry a **global time function** — in any index whose cells are transitions subject to g ≤ q ≤ k, occupancy is non-increasing along composition, closed timelike curves exist exactly within its level sets, and every step of one is conservative. The proof is one line, uses no caps, and is demonstrated capable of failing. **A precedent search, run late, located the content**: a weight decreasing along every edge of a directed graph is a standard object, and semilattice-graded semigroups carry the same shape. What is not located is the derivation — that an index's own counting constraints supply such a grading whether or not anyone puts one there. §6.1 records the demotion.")

anchor="## 7. Λ₉ measured, and it agrees"
assert S.count(anchor)==1
S=S.replace(anchor, """### 6.1 The precedent, found late, and what it costs

§E.7's protocol is *search before deriving*. It was not followed here either: the theorem above was derived, tested at four cap settings, and only then searched. The search located the content.

A weight that falls along every edge of a directed graph, forbidding cycles, is standard and named — an **ℝ-grading on a DAG**, defined as a number at each vertex decreasing by at least one along each edge. Closer still, semigroup theory carries the graded form directly: a homomorphism from a semigroup to a semilattice grades the semigroup so that S_a·S_b ⊆ S_{a∧b}. And Λ₉'s algebraic type outside its top era is named too — a **semigroupoid**, which behaves like a category and lacks identities.

**So the theorem's content is not new, and the paper does not claim it.** What the search did not return is the derivation: that the counting constraints of an index — *cannot remove more than are present*, *cannot place more than were removed* — automatically supply such a grading, so that **any** index of transitions carries a clock whether or not one was put there. That is the narrow residue, and by §27.1 the absence of a source for it is not evidence.

This is the tenth entry in §E.5's ledger of results derived from scratch and found already in print. The mechanism is unchanged and so is the remedy.

""" + anchor)

# ---- 2. move the Precedent part to the end, renumbering 23,24 -> 36,37 ----
i=S.index("# PART V — THE PRECEDENT"); j=S.index("# PART VI — THE REGISTER OF THIS SESSION")
prec=S[i:j]; S=S[:i]+"@@PRECEDENT@@"+S[j:]
prec=prec.replace("# PART V — THE PRECEDENT","# PART IX — THE PRECEDENT")
prec=prec.replace("## 23. The object is Brylawski's","## 36. The object is Brylawski's")
prec=prec.replace("## 24. What this costs, and what survives","## 37. What this costs, and what survives")
prec=prec.replace("the correct name for what §21 proves","the correct name for what §21 proves")
S=S.replace("# PART VI — THE REGISTER OF THIS SESSION","# PART X — THE REGISTER OF THIS SESSION")
S=S.replace("@@PRECEDENT@@","@@NEWPARTS@@\n\n"+prec)
open('paper.md','w',encoding='utf-8').write(S)
print("demotion written, precedent moved to Part IX, placeholder set")
print("placeholder present:", "@@NEWPARTS@@" in S)
PY

# PART V — PAST, PRESENT, FUTURE

## 23. The balance, and where it holds

§10.2 reads the constraint tree as *past — change — future*, left to right: the source end (n, ℓ, k, 2S), the transfer q, the target end (e, f, g). The three-part reading is the book's; what follows is its arithmetic.

**The three parts do not add up as three free things.**

$$|A| \cdot |Q| \cdot |B| = 33 \cdot 4 \cdot 17 = 2{,}244 \qquad \text{against} \qquad |\Lambda| = 976$$

A defect of **1,268** — the three parts overcount by 130% when treated as independent. Conditioned on the transfer they separate exactly: Σ_q |A(q)|·|B(q)| = 976, defect zero.

**And the balance is not special to the transfer.** Tested at every cut of the constraint tree, four of the eight coordinates split it in two — ℓ, q, f and g — and **all four give defect zero.** §12.6.1 presents the q-factorisation as though the transfer were doing the work; the computation says the **tree** is doing it, and q is distinguished only by *which* two things it separates.

**The shape is a path, not a triangle.** Reading the three parts off the constraint tree gives edges past ↔ present and present ↔ future, and **no past–future edge**. Two edges, treewidth 1. That is not decoration: §18.4.1's criterion is that treewidth 1 closes exactly and treewidth 2 gives an envelope, so **Λ's exactness is a proof that the three parts are not a triangle.** A triangle would be the three-body shape, and register 316 states its price.

## 24. The future is a bracket, and the past does not enter

Two questions with computable answers: is the future a function of past and present, and does the past enter at all?

| | |
|---|---|
| (past, present) pairs | 97 |
| futures per pair | min 5 · median 10 · max 17 |
| **pairs determining a single future** | **0 of 97** |

**Not one pair determines a future.** That is §20.1's bracket arriving at the level of the transition itself, and §13.4's line computed — structure does not choose, and 1,113,045,672 maximal chains satisfy every constraint in the book while it chooses none of them.

**And for each value of the present, all pasts give the same future set.**

| present q | distinct pasts | distinct future sets | \|future\| |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 33 | **1** | 5 |
| 1 | 33 | **1** | 10 |
| 2 | 23 | **1** | 15 |
| 3 | 8 | **1** | 17 |

> **The future is conditionally independent of the past given the present.** A Markov property, exact at every value.

That is the arithmetic behind §23's balance: the factorisation *is* the conditional independence, and the 1,268 is what treating the three parts as free costs. The past constrains only which presents are reachable — q ≤ k — and having spent that, it has spent everything.

**The dependence is monotone and opposed.** The future set is **nested increasing** in the present — 5 ⊂ 10 ⊂ 15 ⊂ 17, each containing the last — while the past set is **nested decreasing** — 33 ⊇ 33 ⊇ 23 ⊇ 8. §12.8.1's Pareto frontier, and the same shape as dw/dh > 0 with dV/dh < 0.

**And the bracket is saturated.** At every value of the present the admissible future set is the *full* interval of the target lattice between its own extremes, [(1,0,0), (3,1,q)] — nothing inside is missing. E(X) = 0 read on the target end.

The clock is occupancy and the tick is k − g. Over the 1,169 composable cells of Λ₉:

| tick | cells | share |
|---|---|---|
| 0 — reversible | 389 | 33.3% |
| 1 | 540 | 46.2% |
| 2 | 240 | 20.5% |

**The tick has two sources and they are exactly balanced.** k − g = (k − q) + (q − g): something not removed, and something removed but not placed.

| | cells | share |
|---|---|---|
| something not removed, k > q | **430** | 36.8% |
| something removed and not placed, q > g | **430** | 36.8% |

Not approximately — 430 against 430, with the split table its own transpose: (0,1) = 270 against (1,0) = 270, and (0,2) = 80 against (2,0) = 80. **Irreversibility has two independent sources contributing identically.** One is a choice not taken; the other is a capacity that could not receive.

**And Pauli is a minority partner in the tick.** g's ceiling is fixed by counting in 60.2% of composable cells, tied in 29.5%, and by the shell capacity in **10.3%** — with only 6.2% where Pauli holds g down and the transfer would have allowed more. **The arrow of time in this object is overwhelmingly a counting phenomenon**, which §12.9 states in advance: the coupling g ≤ q binds 35.6% of intervals and g ≤ 4f+2 binds 4.9%.

# PART VI — WHAT CANNOT BE REMOVED

## 26. Pushback

For a cell x, count the pairs of *other* cells that produce it — J(x) joining to x, M(x) meeting at x. Remove x and that is exactly how many pairs of survivors fail.

| | |
|---|---|
| minimum over all 976 cells | **16** |
| median | 506 |
| maximum | 5,091 |
| mean | 739 |
| **cells removable with no failing pair** | **0** |

**No cell of Λ₈ can be removed without the remainder contradicting the removal.** The weakest is implied back sixteen ways.

**The formula is exact rather than fitted.** J(x) recomputed using only the cells at or below x agrees with the global count on 930 of 930 cells checked; M(x) inside [x, ⊤] on 934 of 934. So J(x) is the number of ways x's own down-set is covered by two proper down-subsets, and M(x) the dual: **pushback is a property of the interval and of nothing outside it.**

Which is why statistics fail — corr(pushback, cells below) = +0.425, cells above +0.454, their product +0.117. §16.8.4 found precisely this for insertion: four statistical measures of a constraint all failed and only a measure of the *tree* succeeded. Same shape, second operation.

**J(x) = 0 exactly on the join-irreducibles and M(x) = 0 exactly on the meet-irreducibles**, both exactly, 17 each with ⊥ and ⊤ excluded — reproducing §8.3's count by a route with nothing to do with Birkhoff.

**And the distribution is U-shaped in rank.** Median pushback runs 3,234 at rank 3, down to 335 at rank 10, back up to 1,555 at rank 20. **An index's resistance to deletion is weakest where it is widest** — rank 11 holds 122 cells and defends each of them least — which is the opposite of the intuition that more neighbours means more redundancy.

## 27. The step law

A single cell cannot leave. The minimum that can is derived rather than measured.

*Derivation.* Let R = [a,b] and suppose z ∈ R with z = x∨y and x, y ∉ R. Since x, y ≤ z ≤ b, being outside R means x ≱ a and y ≱ a, while a ≤ x∨y. In a distributive lattice every join-irreducible is join-**prime**, so a ≤ x∨y forces a ≤ x or a ≤ y — contradiction. Conversely if a is join-reducible, a = u∨v with u, v < a, both under b and neither above a, so u, v ∉ R while u∨v = a ∈ R. Dually for meets and b. ∎

> **X ∖ [a,b] is a sublattice if and only if a is join-prime and b is meet-prime.**
>
> **step(X) = min { |[a,b]| : a join-prime, b meet-prime, a ≤ b, 1 < |[a,b]| < |X| }**

**Corrected by its own test.** The first statement of the criterion used *irreducible* rather than *prime* and disagreed with the truth on **35 of 116,138 intervals** — exactly 17 + 17 + 1, being the intervals [⊥, b] with b meet-irreducible, [a, ⊤] with a join-irreducible, and the whole lattice. Convention excludes ⊥ from the join-irreducibles; the property the proof uses is primeness, which ⊥ satisfies trivially. **With *prime*: 0 disagreements in 116,138 intervals**, exhaustive.

| caps | \|Λ\| | \|J\| = \|M\| | doubly irreducible | **step** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (3,3,1,3) | 976 | 17 | **0** | 4 |
| (3,3,1,4) | 1,636 | 21 | **0** | 4 |
| (4,4,1,3) | 1,968 | 19 | **0** | 9 |
| (4,4,1,4) | 3,363 | 23 | **0** | 9 |
| (5,5,1,3) | 3,304 | 21 | **0** | 16 |

At the book's caps the step is a coordinate box free in exactly two coordinates — **n and e, the two shell coordinates, the two ends of the caterpillar** — running from (2,1,3,3,2,1,3,0) to (3,1,3,3,3,1,3,0), and removing it leaves 972 cells with **0 join/meet failures across all 471,906 surviving pairs**.

The step is (n_max − 1)(e_max − 1) at all five settings. That is a pattern across five points and it is **not promoted**: §20.1.2 forbids taking the next term from the pattern the terms make. What is derived is the criterion; a closed form for the minimum over primes is not.

## 28. No cell is doubly irreducible

The two results of §26 and §27 are one fact seen twice.

|[a,a]| = 1 requires a cell that is both join-prime and meet-prime. **Λ has none, at every cap tested** — 17 join-irreducibles, 17 meet-irreducibles, intersection empty. So the pushback floor of 16 and the step of 4 are the same statement: there is no cell whose removal the rest of the index does not contradict, because there is no cell that is irreducible on both sides.

**And the E1 puncture is placed by it.** §12.11.6 removes the one cell nature forbids from the E1 selection rule and reports closure failing by exactly four meets, all four producing the removed cell. Recomputed at cap 20: **0 join failures, 4 meet failures, all four producing (0,0).** Four is not typical — it is near the floor. **The forbidden cell is among the least-defended its index has, and the index still refuses to lose it.**

# PART VII — THE ONE COUPLING

## 29. The cut law

Opposed monotonicity — two quantities moving oppositely under one free parameter — appears at least nine times in *The Method 1.3* and this session, and is never grouped: §12.8.1's Pareto frontier, §21.5.2's dw/dh against dV/dh, §12.11.1's *tree or tightness*, §12.11.0.1's fill against surplus, §6.3's calendar, §17.4's coverage against order, §21.10.3's precision against robustness, §29.3.3's Hodge slice, §30.4.1's paradox-freedom against expressive power, and §24 above.

The lattice-internal instances are derivable.

> **At a cut of the constraint graph on coordinate v, each surviving component shrinks if it contains a parent of v, grows if it contains a child of v, and is flat if it contains neither.** Raising v raises the floor on its parents and the ceiling on its children.

**Tested across all seven stages of the tower and every cut: 89 component tests, one violation.** And the violation is at **Λ₉′**, whose constraint graph is the only one in the tower carrying a cycle — f–g–2S′, the tightening §12.11.1 prices at 93 cells and calls *the tree or the tightness*. The law is a theorem about trees and fails at exactly the stage that stopped being one.

**A prior version of this claim was wrong and is withdrawn.** It read *opposition fails at two-parent coordinates*, which holds at Λ₈ and nowhere above. The cause is not two parents: at Λ₈ the coordinate g has two parents **and no child**, so every component holds a parent and every one shrinks. From Λ₉ onward g has the child 2S′ and opposition returns.

## 30. The two-parent coordinate at every stage of the tower

§11.5 names g ≤ min(q, 4f+2) *the one coupling, and it is the Pauli principle* — the only non-product term in the whole expression. The tower confirms it is the only one anywhere.

| stage | \|X\| | two-parent coordinates | cut behaviour at g |
|---|---|---|---|
| Λ₈ | 976 | **g** | all components shrink |
| Λ₉ | 1,654 | g | opposed |
| Λ₉′ | 1,561 | g **and 2S′** | the one law violation |
| Λ₁₀ | 2,535 | g | opposed |
| Λ₁₁ | 13,585 | g | opposed |
| Λ₁₂ | 70,905 | g | opposed |
| Λ₁₃ | 199,130 | g | opposed |

**g is the unique two-parent bound in the entire tower as built.** Every coordinate from the ninth axis to the thirteenth enters with exactly one parent, which is why closure survives thirteen dimensions and forty-seven million ambient cells.

**And the two places a second could have entered are the two places the book records a price.** Λ₉′ makes 2S′ two-parent — 93 cells bought, the tree lost, and the only violation of the cut law in the run. Λ₁₂'s law for K is 2K ≤ 2J_c + 2f with the cell's own f, and §12.11.3.1 records the book substituting f_max to keep one parent and the cylinder.

## 31. Every second bridge, at the top of the tower

§17's twenty candidates at Λ₈ are repeated at Λ₁₃ with sixty-four.

**As built the factorisation over q is exact at Λ₁₃ — defect 0 on 199,130 cells**, with sections 11,470 · 45,880 · 89,700 · 52,080 reproducing §12.11.5's printed table to the cell.

**Fifty-eight of sixty-four second bridges destroy it**, defects from 1,794 to 82,680. The six that do not are the six that reduce the object to a remnant — k ≤ g at 27.1% of the cells, down to k ≤ f at 2.5%. Register 333's caution: a set cut hard enough factorises trivially.

> **The bridge is one-dimensional not because the index has one dimension available, but because the physics supplies one demand and the construction refuses the second.**

Structurally a second bridge is always admissible — closure survives all sixty-four, as §14.4 guarantees for monotone single-coordinate bounds. Physically the tower offers exactly one: **2K ≤ 2J_c + 2f**, core angular momentum to target orbital momentum. Dimensions 1–10 are single-parent laws, dimension 11 takes its bound from k alone, dimension 13 from K alone.

**And q is the unique cut vertex separating the two ends.** The path from g to K runs **g — q — k — 2J_c — K**, and removing q disconnects them; the cycle the tight K would create is **K — 2J_c — k — q — g — f — K**, length six. The forbidden bridge does not add a new connection between the ends. It adds a *second* one, which is what a tree forbids.

## 32. The tight K, and a discrepancy

§12.11.5 states that the tight two-parent K breaks the factorisation by **2,475 cells, 3.5% of the product**. Recomputed here by four disjoint routes:

| route | Λ₁₂ | Λ₁₃ |
|---|---|---|
| cells cut by restoring the law | **15,150** | **45,450** |
| factorisation defect once restored | **15,150** | **45,450** |
| per-section defect, summed | — | 2,934 + 11,736 + 22,140 + 8,640 = **45,450** |
| three alternative A/B splits | — | 113,325 · 405,715 · 428,340 |

Four routes agree; **none produces 2,475**. What does is arithmetic on the stated percentage: 3.5% × 70,905 = **2,482**. So the two figures printed side by side appear to be one measurement written twice, which is §2.8's vacuous identity — computed along one path, it cannot disagree with itself.

**The rebuild is cleared under §4.1.** It reproduces all seven tower cell counts, the four-cap sweep, the composition closure at 41,682 pairs, and §12.11.5's own four sections exactly.

**The true fraction is 21.4% at Λ₁₂ and 22.8% at Λ₁₃** — and it is not constant: at f_max = 2 the cost rises to **35.3%**. The price of keeping the tree grows with the shell the index carries, which is §12.11.1's density behaviour in a second guise and which neither the book nor this session had before.

Two possibilities remain and the triangulation does not settle between them: 3.5% may measure something narrower than *the product* that this rebuild has not reconstructed, or the cylinder costs six times what the section states. Recorded as a discrepancy to localise rather than a correction to claim.

---

# PART VIII — TWO INDICES

## 33. The reversal

Reversing time is not a sign change. Extending k, q and g below zero was tested at three settings — k ≥ 0, then all three to −1, then to −2 — and the object stays closed (0 join/meet failures) while **0 cells have g > k and 0 steps raise occupancy**, the lattice growing from 976 to 2,691. Neither §7.3's closure proof nor the occupancy law uses positivity. **A negative occupancy is not a reversed one; it is a lower one.**

The reversal is a different object. Exchange the two ends of Λ₉ — (n,ℓ,k,2S) ↔ (e,f,g,2S′), transfer unchanged:

| | |
|---|---|
| \|Λ₉\| | 1,654 |
| \|rev(Λ₉)\| | 1,654 |
| reverse(Λ₉) closed | **yes**, 0 failures |
| **\|Λ₉ ∩ rev(Λ₉)\|** | **389** |

**The reversed index is a lawful closed index of the same size and it is not Λ₉.** That is §8.4's failure of self-duality read temporally: the two are both lawful and simply not the same object.

## 34. The intersection is a groupoid

Every cell of the intersection satisfies **g = q = k** — total transfer, nothing left behind — and the intersection is the reversible region twice over: it is exactly the 389 morphisms carrying a reverse.

| position | cells | join fail | meet fail | E(X) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Λ₉ forward | 1,654 | 0 | 0 | **0** |
| rev(Λ₉) backward | 1,654 | 0 | 0 | **0** |
| **Λ₉ ∩ rev(Λ₉)** | **389** | **0** | **0** | **0** |

**And it is a groupoid, entire.** 4,887 composable pairs with zero closure failures; **all 33 objects carry a genuine identity; all 389 morphisms have a two-sided inverse.** Λ₉ is a category and a groupoid only at its top; the intersection *is* the groupoid.

It carries its own transfer and factorises exactly — Σ_q |A(q)|·|B(q)| = 389 against 389, defect zero — so the whole construction reproduces one level down.

> **The second present definable from the forward and backward indices is the region in which time has no direction, and it is 23.5% of Λ₉.**

This unifies two results reported separately. §7's cycles were confined to level sets of occupancy with every step conservative; conservative is g = q and the level-set condition is k = g. **The intersection is that condition stated as an object rather than as a property of paths.**

## 35. The union does not exist

| position | cells | join fail | meet fail | E(X) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Λ₉ ∪ rev(Λ₉) | 2,919 | **360,000** | **470,625** | **2,857** |

Three of the four positions exist and the fourth does not. **The top is missing.** A present is definable from the past and future indices; the thing containing both is not.

That is not a technicality. §17's E1 admits cells when their joins and meets fall back inside; here **2,857 further cells** would have to be admitted, and §16.8.4's amplification is exactly that cost. **A structure containing both directions of time is not available at any price the index recognises** — only a structure containing their agreement.

Which is why statistics fail — corr(pushback, cells below) = +0.425, cells above +0.454, their product +0.117. §16.8.4 found precisely this for insertion: four statistical measures of a constraint all failed and only a measure of the *tree* succeeded. Same shape, second operation.

**J(x) = 0 exactly on the join-irreducibles and M(x) = 0 exactly on the meet-irreducibles**, both exactly, 17 each with ⊥ and ⊤ excluded — reproducing §8.3's count by a route with nothing to do with Birkhoff.

**And the distribution is U-shaped in rank.** Median pushback runs 3,234 at rank 3, down to 335 at rank 10, back up to 1,555 at rank 20. **An index's resistance to deletion is weakest where it is widest** — rank 11 holds 122 cells and defends each of them least — which is the opposite of the intuition that more neighbours means more redundancy.

## 27. The step law

A single cell cannot leave. The minimum that can is derived rather than measured.

*Derivation.* Let R = [a,b] and suppose z ∈ R with z = x∨y and x, y ∉ R. Since x, y ≤ z ≤ b, being outside R means x ≱ a and y ≱ a, while a ≤ x∨y. In a distributive lattice every join-irreducible is join-**prime**, so a ≤ x∨y forces a ≤ x or a ≤ y — contradiction. Conversely if a is join-reducible, a = u∨v with u, v < a, both under b and neither above a, so u, v ∉ R while u∨v = a ∈ R. Dually for meets and b. ∎

> **X ∖ [a,b] is a sublattice if and only if a is join-prime and b is meet-prime.**
>
> **step(X) = min { |[a,b]| : a join-prime, b meet-prime, a ≤ b, 1 < |[a,b]| < |X| }**

**Corrected by its own test.** The first statement of the criterion used *irreducible* rather than *prime* and disagreed with the truth on **35 of 116,138 intervals** — exactly 17 + 17 + 1, being the intervals [⊥, b] with b meet-irreducible, [a, ⊤] with a join-irreducible, and the whole lattice. Convention excludes ⊥ from the join-irreducibles; the property the proof uses is primeness, which ⊥ satisfies trivially. **With *prime*: 0 disagreements in 116,138 intervals**, exhaustive.

| caps | \|Λ\| | \|J\| = \|M\| | doubly irreducible | **step** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (3,3,1,3) | 976 | 17 | **0** | 4 |
| (3,3,1,4) | 1,636 | 21 | **0** | 4 |
| (4,4,1,3) | 1,968 | 19 | **0** | 9 |
| (4,4,1,4) | 3,363 | 23 | **0** | 9 |
| (5,5,1,3) | 3,304 | 21 | **0** | 16 |

At the book's caps the step is a coordinate box free in exactly two coordinates — **n and e, the two shell coordinates, the two ends of the caterpillar** — running from (2,1,3,3,2,1,3,0) to (3,1,3,3,3,1,3,0), and removing it leaves 972 cells with **0 join/meet failures across all 471,906 surviving pairs**.

The step is (n_max − 1)(e_max − 1) at all five settings. That is a pattern across five points and it is **not promoted**: §20.1.2 forbids taking the next term from the pattern the terms make. What is derived is the criterion; a closed form for the minimum over primes is not.

## 28. No cell is doubly irreducible

The two results of §26 and §27 are one fact seen twice.

|[a,a]| = 1 requires a cell that is both join-prime and meet-prime. **Λ has none, at every cap tested** — 17 join-irreducibles, 17 meet-irreducibles, intersection empty. So the pushback floor of 16 and the step of 4 are the same statement: there is no cell whose removal the rest of the index does not contradict, because there is no cell that is irreducible on both sides.

**And the E1 puncture is placed by it.** §12.11.6 removes the one cell nature forbids from the E1 selection rule and reports closure failing by exactly four meets, all four producing the removed cell. Recomputed at cap 20: **0 join failures, 4 meet failures, all four producing (0,0).** Four is not typical — it is near the floor. **The forbidden cell is among the least-defended its index has, and the index still refuses to lose it.**

---

# PART VII — THE ONE COUPLING

## 29. The cut law

Opposed monotonicity — two quantities moving oppositely under one free parameter — appears at least nine times in *The Method 1.3* and this session, and is never grouped: §12.8.1's Pareto frontier, §21.5.2's dw/dh against dV/dh, §12.11.1's *tree or tightness*, §12.11.0.1's fill against surplus, §6.3's calendar, §17.4's coverage against order, §21.10.3's precision against robustness, §29.3.3's Hodge slice, §30.4.1's paradox-freedom against expressive power, and §24 above.

The lattice-internal instances are derivable.

> **At a cut of the constraint graph on coordinate v, each surviving component shrinks if it contains a parent of v, grows if it contains a child of v, and is flat if it contains neither.** Raising v raises the floor on its parents and the ceiling on its children.

**Tested across all seven stages of the tower and every cut: 89 component tests, one violation.** And the violation is at **Λ₉′**, whose constraint graph is the only one in the tower carrying a cycle — f–g–2S′, the tightening §12.11.1 prices at 93 cells and calls *the tree or the tightness*. The law is a theorem about trees and fails at exactly the stage that stopped being one.

**A prior version of this claim was wrong and is withdrawn.** It read *opposition fails at two-parent coordinates*, which holds at Λ₈ and nowhere above. The cause is not two parents: at Λ₈ the coordinate g has two parents **and no child**, so every component holds a parent and every one shrinks. From Λ₉ onward g has the child 2S′ and opposition returns.

## 30. The two-parent coordinate at every stage of the tower

§11.5 names g ≤ min(q, 4f+2) *the one coupling, and it is the Pauli principle* — the only non-product term in the whole expression. The tower confirms it is the only one anywhere.

| stage | \|X\| | two-parent coordinates | cut behaviour at g |
|---|---|---|---|
| Λ₈ | 976 | **g** | all components shrink |
| Λ₉ | 1,654 | g | opposed |
| Λ₉′ | 1,561 | g **and 2S′** | the one law violation |
| Λ₁₀ | 2,535 | g | opposed |
| Λ₁₁ | 13,585 | g | opposed |
| Λ₁₂ | 70,905 | g | opposed |
| Λ₁₃ | 199,130 | g | opposed |

**g is the unique two-parent bound in the entire tower as built.** Every coordinate from the ninth axis to the thirteenth enters with exactly one parent, which is why closure survives thirteen dimensions and forty-seven million ambient cells.

**And the two places a second could have entered are the two places the book records a price.** Λ₉′ makes 2S′ two-parent — 93 cells bought, the tree lost, and the only violation of the cut law in the run. Λ₁₂'s law for K is 2K ≤ 2J_c + 2f with the cell's own f, and §12.11.3.1 records the book substituting f_max to keep one parent and the cylinder.

## 31. Every second bridge, at the top of the tower

§17's twenty candidates at Λ₈ are repeated at Λ₁₃ with sixty-four.

**As built the factorisation over q is exact at Λ₁₃ — defect 0 on 199,130 cells**, with sections 11,470 · 45,880 · 89,700 · 52,080 reproducing §12.11.5's printed table to the cell.

**Fifty-eight of sixty-four second bridges destroy it**, defects from 1,794 to 82,680. The six that do not are the six that reduce the object to a remnant — k ≤ g at 27.1% of the cells, down to k ≤ f at 2.5%. Register 333's caution: a set cut hard enough factorises trivially.

> **The bridge is one-dimensional not because the index has one dimension available, but because the physics supplies one demand and the construction refuses the second.**

Structurally a second bridge is always admissible — closure survives all sixty-four, as §14.4 guarantees for monotone single-coordinate bounds. Physically the tower offers exactly one: **2K ≤ 2J_c + 2f**, core angular momentum to target orbital momentum. Dimensions 1–10 are single-parent laws, dimension 11 takes its bound from k alone, dimension 13 from K alone.

**And q is the unique cut vertex separating the two ends.** The path from g to K runs **g — q — k — 2J_c — K**, and removing q disconnects them; the cycle the tight K would create is **K — 2J_c — k — q — g — f — K**, length six. The forbidden bridge does not add a new connection between the ends. It adds a *second* one, which is what a tree forbids.

## 32. The tight K, and a discrepancy

§12.11.5 states that the tight two-parent K breaks the factorisation by **2,475 cells, 3.5% of the product**. Recomputed here by four disjoint routes:

| route | Λ₁₂ | Λ₁₃ |
|---|---|---|
| cells cut by restoring the law | **15,150** | **45,450** |
| factorisation defect once restored | **15,150** | **45,450** |
| per-section defect, summed | — | 2,934 + 11,736 + 22,140 + 8,640 = **45,450** |
| three alternative A/B splits | — | 113,325 · 405,715 · 428,340 |

Four routes agree; **none produces 2,475**. What does is arithmetic on the stated percentage: 3.5% × 70,905 = **2,482**. So the two figures printed side by side appear to be one measurement written twice, which is §2.8's vacuous identity — computed along one path, it cannot disagree with itself.

**The rebuild is cleared under §4.1.** It reproduces all seven tower cell counts, the four-cap sweep, the composition closure at 41,682 pairs, and §12.11.5's own four sections exactly.

**The true fraction is 21.4% at Λ₁₂ and 22.8% at Λ₁₃** — and it is not constant: at f_max = 2 the cost rises to **35.3%**. The price of keeping the tree grows with the shell the index carries, which is §12.11.1's density behaviour in a second guise and which neither the book nor this session had before.

Two possibilities remain and the triangulation does not settle between them: 3.5% may measure something narrower than *the product* that this rebuild has not reconstructed, or the cylinder costs six times what the section states. Recorded as a discrepancy to localise rather than a correction to claim.

---

# PART VIII — TWO INDICES

## 33. The reversal

Reversing time is not a sign change. Extending k, q and g below zero was tested at three settings — k ≥ 0, then all three to −1, then to −2 — and the object stays closed (0 join/meet failures) while **0 cells have g > k and 0 steps raise occupancy**, the lattice growing from 976 to 2,691. Neither §7.3's closure proof nor the occupancy law uses positivity. **A negative occupancy is not a reversed one; it is a lower one.**

The reversal is a different object. Exchange the two ends of Λ₉ — (n,ℓ,k,2S) ↔ (e,f,g,2S′), transfer unchanged:

| | |
|---|---|
| \|Λ₉\| | 1,654 |
| \|rev(Λ₉)\| | 1,654 |
| reverse(Λ₉) closed | **yes**, 0 failures |
| **\|Λ₉ ∩ rev(Λ₉)\|** | **389** |

**The reversed index is a lawful closed index of the same size and it is not Λ₉.** That is §8.4's failure of self-duality read temporally: the two are both lawful and simply not the same object.

## 34. The intersection is a groupoid

Every cell of the intersection satisfies **g = q = k** — total transfer, nothing left behind — and the intersection is the reversible region twice over: it is exactly the 389 morphisms carrying a reverse.

| position | cells | join fail | meet fail | E(X) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Λ₉ forward | 1,654 | 0 | 0 | **0** |
| rev(Λ₉) backward | 1,654 | 0 | 0 | **0** |
| **Λ₉ ∩ rev(Λ₉)** | **389** | **0** | **0** | **0** |

**And it is a groupoid, entire.** 4,887 composable pairs with zero closure failures; **all 33 objects carry a genuine identity; all 389 morphisms have a two-sided inverse.** Λ₉ is a category and a groupoid only at its top; the intersection *is* the groupoid.

It carries its own transfer and factorises exactly — Σ_q |A(q)|·|B(q)| = 389 against 389, defect zero — so the whole construction reproduces one level down.

> **The second present definable from the forward and backward indices is the region in which time has no direction, and it is 23.5% of Λ₉.**

This unifies two results reported separately. §7's cycles were confined to level sets of occupancy with every step conservative; conservative is g = q and the level-set condition is k = g. **The intersection is that condition stated as an object rather than as a property of paths.**

## 35. The union does not exist

| position | cells | join fail | meet fail | E(X) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Λ₉ ∪ rev(Λ₉) | 2,919 | **360,000** | **470,625** | **2,857** |

Three of the four positions exist and the fourth does not. **The top is missing.** A present is definable from the past and future indices; the thing containing both is not.

That is not a technicality. §17's E1 admits cells when their joins and meets fall back inside; here **2,857 further cells** would have to be admitted, and §16.8.4's amplification is exactly that cost. **A structure containing both directions of time is not available at any price the index recognises** — only a structure containing their agreement.

Caught up. **30 pages, 15,800 words, ten parts, twelve figures — fifteen audits run, fifteen pass, zero render warnings.**

**What's new.** Four parts, sections 23–35. **Part V — Past, Present, Future**: the balance holding at four cuts not one, the path-not-triangle proof, the Markov property, the future as a saturated interval, and the tick's 430/430 split. **Part VI — What Cannot Be Removed**: pushback with its floor of 16, the step law derived and corrected by its own test, and the unification — no cell is doubly irreducible, which is why the floor is never zero and the step never one. **Part VII — The One Coupling**: the cut law at 89 tests with its single violation, g as the unique two-parent bound at all seven stages, the 64 bridges at Λ₁₃, and the tight-K discrepancy. **Part VIII — Two Indices**: the reversal, the groupoid at 389 cells, and the union that does not close.

**The n-body work is retained in full**, Part IV intact, and the abstract now says why — it is the route by which everything after it was reached. The Brylawski precedent stays as Part IX rather than being softened.

**The headline was demoted.** §6.1 is new: the occupancy clock was derived, tested at four caps, written up, and only then searched — and the search found the content. DAG gradings and semilattice-graded semigroups carry the same shape, and *semigroupoid* is the standing name for what Λ₉ is outside its top era. The narrow residue is the derivation, not the object. Tenth entry in §E.5's ledger, and §E.7's protocol reversed twice in one session.

**The register runs to eighteen**, six of them new withdrawals: the clock claimed before it was searched, the balance predicted at one cut and holding at four, opposition attributed to two parents, *irreducible* where the proof needs *prime*, a cut test that skipped the case it existed for, and a crossing called a coincidence.

**And entry 18 is the one I'd point at.** The expansion broke five audits and none of them was the paper — a single-digit regex for figure references, the same literal again for captions, a hardcoded image count, a part name the renumbering moved, an appendix boundary. **Eleven instrument repairs against the paper's five**, across this session. The book records the mechanism three times; there are now eleven more, and the flat statement seems worth having: *an instrument written against an object encodes the object's current size, and the next edit is what finds it.*

content.text:
All four are my probe, not the paper: pandoc converts the straight apostrophe to a typographic one, so `cylinder's` in source is `cylinder’s` in the artefact. The same normalisation the PROJECTION check already applies, absent from this one. With it applied the count is 12 of 12.

**Twelve captions, twelve bodies, fifty-eight headings, twenty-four images, thirty pages, zero missing glyphs.**

The underlying defect was real and worth naming. **Figure 3's caption was absent from the artefact entirely** — label and body — while the source was perfect and every source-side audit passed. The cause was float migration: pandoc's implicit-figure conversion makes each image a LaTeX float, two floats landed on page 8, and the second one's caption was lost. Rebuilding with `-f markdown-implicit_figures` makes the images inline, which fixes it and also removes the duplicated "Figure 2: Figure 2" labels the float mechanism was generating.

**This is register 190's class exactly** — *an audit that reads the wrong artefact will pass anything*. My COHERENCE check compared figure references to captions **in the source**, so it verified that twelve captions existed in a file where they always existed. Nothing in the suite read the rendered page for caption presence. The check that found it was the three-file agreement test I ran only because you asked for the audit again.

Publishing the corrected build and adding the missing check.

from itertools import product

# obstacle: 0 retrievable · 1 buildable · 2 requires an object that does not exist
# cost    : 0 hours · 1 days · 2 unbounded
items={
 "O1 occupancy-law precedent":   (1,0,1,"bibliographic"),
 "O2 E(X) on the dominance order":(1,0,2,"bibliographic"),
 "O6 step-law precedent":        (1,0,1,"bibliographic"),
 "O3 the density trend in n":    (0,1,1,"structural"),
 "O4 composition above the ninth":(0,1,1,"structural"),
 "O8 an observable under E2":    (0,1,0,"structural"),
 "O5 the tight-K discrepancy":   (0,0,0,"computational"),
 "O7 the three defects of §4":   (0,0,0,"computational"),
}
def R(X,d=3):
    A=[sorted({x[i] for x in X}) for i in range(d)]
    phi={(i,j):{v:(max([x[i] for x in X if x[j]<=v]) if any(x[j]<=v for x in X) else None)
                for v in A[j]} for i in range(d) for j in range(d) if i!=j}
    return [y for y in product(*A) if all(phi[(i,j)][y[j]] is not None and y[i]<=phi[(i,j)][y[j]]
            for i in range(d) for j in range(d) if i!=j)]
cells=[v[:3] for v in items.values()]

Appendix C is rewritten as **Open, closed, and unclosable** — ten items on your three-value scale, and three of them are now actually closed. 32 pages, fifteen audits passing on the delivered files.

**O1 — composition above the ninth axis. Closed, and it reverses the book.** §12.11.0 records composition lost at Λ₁₀ because seniority has no source counterpart. Supplying one — a source seniority w with 2S ≤ w ≤ k, by the identical construction — gives a 5,525-cell closed index whose targets are legal sources 65 of 70 and which **composes on 266,125 pairs with zero failures**. The loss at the tenth axis is a **defect of the construction, not a law**. Register 314's general claim survives; its instance does not.

**O2 — adjunction under E2. Closed.** Against the closed envelope: existing coordinates, max, min and constants all admissible at zero failures; **all three differences forbidden** — S₁₃ at 1,935, S₂₃ at 4,350, m₂ at 4,171. Next, we consider the Min-Max Product problem which was studied in the context of All-Pairs Bottleneck Paths and All-Pairs Nondecreasing Paths. We show that Duan and Pettie's $\tilde{O}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})$ -time algorithm [49] is best-possible (if $\omega = 2$ ), conditioned on the APSP Hypothesis.

**Definition 6.4** (Min-Max Product). The min-max product of two matrices $A, B \in \mathbb{Z}^{n \times n}$ is the matrix $C \in \mathbb{Z}^{n \times n}$ defined by

$$C[i, j] = \min_{k \in [n]} \max\{A[i, k], B[k, j]\}.$$

The Min-Max Product problem is to compute the min-max product of two given matrices A, B.

**Lemma 6.5** (Min-Max Product). Min-Max Product cannot be solved in time $O(n^{2.5-\epsilon})$ (for any constant $\epsilon > 0$ ), unless the APSP Hypothesis fails.



**Proof.** The proof is almost immediate by Lemma 6.3: The min product of two matrices A and B can be expressed as the min-max product of the matrices A and B', where B' is obtained from B by replacing 1 with $-\infty$ and 0 by $\infty$ .

This lower bound entails various other lower bounds. By the known equivalence [95] we conclude our lower bound for All-Pairs Bottleneck Paths (Theorem 1.15). Moreover, from known reductions [96] it follows that also the Min- $\leq$ Product and the All-Pairs Nondecreasing Paths problems cannot be solved in time $O(n^{2.5-\epsilon})$ unless the APSP Hypothesis fails, matching their respective upper bounds if $\omega = 2$ [96, 47, 48]. Lemma 6.5 also implies a matching lower bound for the All-Edges Monochromatic Equality Triangle problem studied in [98].

Given the adjacency or weight matrix of a graph of n vertices, using a 2-d mesh to determine various properties of the graph has long been studied. Thus, the standard graph composition is referred to as the *max-min composition*:

$$P \circ P = \max_{k} \min(p_{ik}, p_{kj}) = p'_{ij}.$$

The transitive closure $P^{T}(X)$ of a graph P(X) can then be defined as:

$$P^T = \bigcup_{\eta=1}^{\kappa} P^{\eta},\tag{2.1}$$

where $P^{\eta} = P \circ P^{\eta-1}$ , for $\eta = 2, 3, ...$ , and $P^1 = P$ [45]. Furthermore, $P \cup Q$ denotes the union of two graphs defined on same node set X and is defined by the disjunction of their respective adjacency matrix entries: $p_{ij} \vee q_{ij}$ , $\forall_{x_i,x_j \in X}$ , where $\vee$ denotes the same t-conorm used in the composition. In the most general case, $\kappa \to \infty$ [38], but when $\vee = \max \min$ , with any t-norm $\wedge$ , we have $\kappa \leq |X| - 1$ [45]. In other words, in the latter case the transitive closure converges in finite time and is easily computed via formula 2.1 [68].

The protocol worked, and cell 4 was the one four whole-statement queries had missed. **Λ₉'s composition law is bottleneck composition, and it has a large named literature.**

Max-min composition is the standard graph composition, P∘P = maxₖ min(p_ik, p_kj), and the algebra it lives in is named: (R, min, max, ∞, −∞) is a closed semiring, also known as the subtropical semiring. The path problem is standard too — all-pairs bottleneck path, also known as the widest path problem, which finds a path maximising the smallest weight on the path — and the reading of q falls straight out of it: the capacity of a path is the minimum capacity of any edge along it, and the minimum-capacity edge forms a bottleneck.

So **q is a capacity, and composing transitions is taking the bottleneck.** §12.6.1 calls q *the conserved coupling*; the sharper statement is that it is the transition's capacity and the composite carries the narrowest one. That reframes register 313's "composition is time" — the clock is occupancy, and the transfer is a capacity composing in the subtropical semiring.

**O6's target index now stands at four of six located**, and the two remaining are the ones actually specific to this work:

content.title: Interval-Dismantling for Lattices
content.text:
## 1 Introduction

The dismantling of elements in ordered sets, in particular that of irreducible elements, was examined for example in [1,3,6,8,9]. Notably, in [3] Duffus and Rival examined the dismantling of doubly irreducible elements and proved the uniqueness of the DI-core, i. e., the poset that remains when all doubly irreducible elements have been removed. In [4] Farley gave a simpler proof relying on results for semimodular posets.

In Formal Concept Analysis (FCA) the removal of a doubly irreducible element in a concept lattice corresponds to the removal of a single incidence (cross) from its (clarified) formal context, cf. [5, Prop. 53]. The dismantling of a doubly irreducible element results in a complete sublattice of the original concept lattice. In particular, this sublattice contains all but one of the original concepts.



In this paper, we extend the notion of dismantling from single elements to intervals in order to remove multiple (not necessarily irreducible) concepts at once while preserving the remaining concept lattice. To this end, we make use of the one-to-one correspondence between closed subrelations of a formal context and the complete sublattices of its concept lattice [10], and, more generally, of the one-to-one correspondence between closed subcontexts of a context and the sublattices of its concept lattice [7].

Extending dismantling to intervals, we call an interval $[u,v] =: \underline{S}$ dismantling for a lattice $\underline{L}$ if v is infimum prime in the filter of u, u is supremum prime in

the ideal of v and $u, v \notin \{\bot, \top\}$ . Because infimum (supremum) prime implies infimum (supremum) irreducible, dismantling intervals that consist of a single element are precisely the doubly irreducible elements.

content.title: On the representation of finite distributive lattices
content.text:
# ON THE REPRESENTATIONS OF FINITE DISTRIBUTIVE LATTICES

## MARK SIGGERS

ABSTRACT. A simple but elegant result of Rival states that every sublattice L of a finite distributive lattice  $\mathcal P$  can be constructed from  $\mathcal P$  by removing a particular family  $\mathcal I_L$  of its irreducible intervals.

Applying this in the case that  $\mathcal{P}$  is a product of a finite set  $\mathcal{C}$  of chains, we get a one-to-one correspondence  $L \mapsto D_{\mathcal{P}}(L)$  between the sublattices of  $\mathcal{P}$  and the preorders spanned by a canonical sublattice  $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$  of  $\mathcal{P}$ .

We then show that L is a tight sublattice of the product of chains  $\mathcal{P}$  if and only if  $D_{\mathcal{P}}(L)$  is asymmetric. This yields a one-to-one correspondence between the tight sublattices of  $\mathcal{P}$  and the posets spanned by its poset  $J(\mathcal{P})$  of non-zero join-irreducible elements.

# ALMOST EVERYWHERE DIVERGENCE OF CESÀRO MEANS OF SUBSEQUENCES OF WALSH-PALEY FOURIER PARTIAL SUMS

## ISTVÁN BLAHOTA AND GYÖRGY GÁT

ABSTRACT. We prove an almost everywhere divergence theorem for Cesàro means of subsequences of partial sums of Walsh–Fourier series. More precisely, we show that there exist a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers $(a_n)$ and a function $f \in L^1(G)$ , where Gdenotes the dyadic group, such that

$$\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_{a_n}f(x)\right)_{N=1}^{\infty}$$

does not converge for almost every $x \in G$ .

The result is motivated by the corresponding trigonometric problem.

A problem going back to Zalcwasser [24] and remaining open for almost ninety years was recently solved in the trigonometric setting by Gát [12], who proved almost everywhere divergence for suitable subsequential arithmetic means of partial sums.

In the Walsh–Paley setting the situation is more delicate. 

The situation is even more delicate if one considers only a subsequence of the partial sums. In the trigonometric setting this question has a very strong negative aspect. Gosselin proved that for every subsequence $(n_j)$ of the positive integers there exists an $f \in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ such that

$$\sup_{j\in\mathbb{P}}|S_{n_j}f|=+\infty$$

almost everywhere. Totik later strengthened this result by obtaining divergence everywhere [13, 23]. Thus, in the trigonometric case, no prescribed subsequence of partial sums can guarantee pointwise convergence for all integrable functions.

<sup>2020</sup> Mathematics Subject Classification. 42C10.

Key words and phrases. Walsh–Fourier series, subsequences of partial sums, Cesàro means, almost everywhere divergence, Walsh–Paley system.

The second author was supported by the University of Debrecen Program for Scientific Publication.

In mathematical analysis, Cesàro summation (also known as the Cesàro mean[1][2] or Cesàro limit[3]) assigns values to some infinite sums that are not necessarily convergent in the usual sense. The Cesàro sum is defined as the limit, as n tends to infinity, of the sequence of arithmetic means of the first n partial sums of the series. This special case of a matrix summability method is named for the Italian analyst Ernesto Cesàro (1859–1906). The term summation can be misleading, as some statements and proofs regarding Cesàro summation can be said to implicate the Eilenberg–Mazur swindle.

## 1 Introduction

By a weight sequence $\{w(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^+}$ , we mean a non-negative sequence of real numbers. We say that a weight sequence $\{w(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^+}$ is in the Ariño -Muckenhoupt discrete weight class $\mathcal{B}_p$ (see [1]), if

there exists a constant c > 0 such that

$$\sum_{k=n}^{\infty} \left(\frac{n}{k}\right)^p w(k) \le c \sum_{k=1}^n w(k) \text{ for all } n \in \mathbb{Z}^+.$$



The continuous version of Theorem B was proved by Carro and Lorente in 2010 [5] for non-negative non-increasing measurable functions with $B_p$ class of weights. The $B_p$ weight class is a continuous version of the discrete $\mathcal{B}_p$ class of weight sequences. A weight w is said to belong to the class $B_p$ (p > 0), if there exists a constant c > 0 such that the inequality

$$\int_{r}^{\infty} \left(\frac{r}{x}\right)^{p} w(x) dx \le c \int_{0}^{r} w(x) dx$$

holds for every r > 0. Let us write

$$[w]_{B_p} := \inf \left\{ c \ge 1 : \int_0^r w(x) dx + \int_r^\infty \left(\frac{r}{x}\right)^p w(x) dx \le c \int_0^r w(x) dx, \ r > 0 \right\}.$$

content.text:
Located, and the vocabulary shift was the whole difficulty.

**The envelope class is *starshaped*.** The classical definition is exactly the Cesàro condition: S(b) = {f : f(x)/x ≤ f(y)/y for 0 < x < y ≤ b}, and Bruckner and Ostrow proved the strict inclusions K(b) ⊂ S(b) ⊂ S̄(b) — convex ⊊ starshaped ⊊ superadditive, *Some function classes related to the class of convex functions*, Pacific J. Math. 12 (1962), 1203–1215. And the discrete case is a named body of work in its own right: Toader's **hierarchies of convexity of sequences**.

So the paper's exact set and envelope are the two ends of a classical strict inclusion, and **the density is the measure of that strictness** — 68.1%, 38.2%, 19.8% at n = 3, 4, 5. The inclusion being strict has been known since 1962; how strict, at each n, was not returned.
